articles.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel conflicts
articles.summary: The world’s food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict. Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many…

blocks.text: The world’s food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict.

Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many regions. A developing El Niño event is even threatening to worsen food shortages for millions of people next year. At the same time, wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting supply chains that keep food and farm supplies moving.
The war in Ukraine has repeatedly shaken grain markets, while the Iran war’s impact on the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel and fertilizer prices, increasing costs for farmers everywhere.

Experts have long warned that rising food insecurity could fuel instability. When people can no longer feed their families, they argue over land, water, and other resources — or they move. In fragile countries, these pressures can contribute to social unrest and even armed conflict.

Now, new research has suggested where some of these risks are greatest. The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI), developed by Laura Mayoral, Hannes Mueller and colleagues, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity around the world. “The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions,” said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and the Barcelona School of Economics.

Climate change is already reducing food production in many parts of the world. Hundreds of millions of people live in areas where harvests are smaller than 30 years ago. Mueller mentioned Australia, Argentina, Moldova, Nigeria, Romania, the United States, and Sudan as countries where agricultural losses are already being felt.
“Northern Africa is another region we should pay much more attention to. If you look at the map, it just looks terrible. It really looks horrible,” he said.
And climate change is only one part of the story. Wars, trade disruptions, export bans, and rising fertilizer costs can magnify food insecurity.
Within the next 25 years, nearly half of the world’s people could be living in areas where farms are producing less food.
New winners, losers, and conflicts

These pressures can undermine governments, help cause migration, and make it easier for armed groups to recruit fighters. In societies that are already unstable, such factors can push them toward crisis.

Yet CADI’s research points to a surprising reality: Gains in agricultural productivity also appear to increase the risk of violence. Mueller said the key issue is not just scarcity, but change. The climate crisis and other shocks do not simply make some regions poorer. They also create new opportunities, changing the value of land and resources.
In some places, land that had been marginal becomes more productive and more valuable. And that attracts investors and produces competition for ownership and access.

So countries that appear to benefit overall may face new tensions. Sudan, for example, is projected to produce more food as the climate changes. But while some areas could become more productive, others may suffer losses, creating new winners and losers within the country and increasing the risk of conflict.

This looming instability, Mueller said, also applies to areas where the change in productivity hasn’t even happened yet. “If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today. That is exactly where negotiations break down and where we will have violence,” he said.

Even in stable, wealthy regions, the climate crisis is creating future problems. It may seem trivial, but the change in grape-growing options in Europe is affecting local farmers. Major producers of sparkling wine have started to buy up land in mountainous regions.

“It is not productive yet, but they already know where future grape harvests will be,” Mueller said. “Big agricultural companies are buying land. This is happening all over the world. Locals are displaced because large producers come in, land prices rise, and you start having fights about something that is still 20 or 30 years in the future.”

One of the CADI team’s most striking findings is that agricultural change is more likely to lead to conflict in non-democracies. When climate shocks, food insecurity, and competition over resources hit democracies, they tend to have institutions that force competing interests to negotiate rather than fight.

“Democracies may look annoying and cumbersome. Nothing moves as fast as people want. But this is a great thing because it makes people talk to each other,” Mueller said. “There is a platform for negotiation. There are institutions that help people negotiate. That process of constantly finding solutions is at the heart of what prevents conflict.”
South Asia as a warning sign

“We do not pay enough attention to the threats to the source of our livelihoods,” said Abdullah Fahimi of the think tank German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). “These threats can trigger major crises and displace millions and millions of people. The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel, where climate vulnerability and rapid population growth mean the number of people affected could rise dramatically.”

blocks.caption: As India counts its population, researchers warn that climate change could make it harder for parts of the country to produce enough food for a growing number of people Image: Diptendu Dutta/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fahimi said South Asia stands out because it depends on both vulnerable water supplies and global food markets. Food prices have already risen significantly over the past decades. “South Asia, with a population of around 2 billion, is highly dependent on imports,” he added. Those imports include wheat, maize, and palm oil from countries including Russia, Ukraine, Canada, and Malaysia.
At the same time, local agriculture is increasingly threatened by heat waves, floods, declining land productivity, and saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels.

As well as the immediate human toll, events such as the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026 offer a glimpse of the long-term challenges that could become more common in the future. “The Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges supply most of the water for agriculture and drinking water in the region,” Fahimi said. “Because of climate change, the glaciers and snow are melting very fast.”
In the short term, meltwater could increase water availability. But later in the century, he warned, the region could face “a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people.”

blocks.caption: Farmland was covered in mud after severe flooding along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River in late August Image: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: As food insecurity deepens, the social and political consequences can multiply. “When resource scarcities or the impacts of climate change force people to look for other livelihood opportunities, sometimes they end up being hired by terrorist groups,” said Fahimi, who cited examples from Nigeria and Afghanistan.

In other cases, public frustration is directed at governments if they fail to mitigate the effects on people’s livelihoods. Their legitimacy is questioned, and this can escalate into violent conflict.

That echoes Mueller’s broader conclusion. Climate change, wars, and trade disruptions do not automatically lead to conflict. But climate adaptation cannot just be about growing different crops or using new technologies. People and societies also need to adapt to changes in who has access to land, water and jobs.

The key question is whether societies have institutions that can manage these changes. Where governments, courts, and local institutions can help communities negotiate new realities, shocks may be absorbed. Where those institutions are weak, the pressure on food systems may become a pressure on peace itself. /dl

articles.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
articles.summary: It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn’t lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs…

blocks.text: It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn’t lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called “the great hunting tick,” was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn’t have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.
Seeking German cooperation
Sherifi got in touch with Germany’s largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

blocks.caption: While the much smaller common longhorn beetle (left) waits for a suitable victim to pass by, the Hyalomma tick prefers to go hunting Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers’ joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country’s Foreign Ministry and “intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats.”

“It’s give and take,” said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. “We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don’t have the patients.” Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.
Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.
“This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected,” Sherifi explained.
Patients require intensive care, isolation
He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

blocks.caption: Farmers in Kosovo are at particular risk from the Hyalomma ticks Image: Idro Seferi

blocks.text: “If you do get sick, it’s particularly severe,” Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.
Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient’s vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, “ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients.” That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it’s also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.
Successful tick tactics

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn’t affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it’s clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.
Of course, that doesn’t mean the ticks and the virus won’t spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.
Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.
“Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically,” said Emmerich. “As a virologist, that’s something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored.”

This is why it’s important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they’ve learned to countries that haven’t yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania. /dl

articles.title: Butuan’s state of calamity declaration to hasten emergency response
articles.summary: SAN FRANCISCO, Surigao del Sur – Butuan City Mayor Lawrence Fortun said the state of calamity declaration will allow the city government to accelerate emergency spending, mobilize more agencies, and…

blocks.text: SAN FRANCISCO, Surigao del Sur – Butuan City Mayor Lawrence Fortun said the state of calamity declaration will allow the city government to accelerate emergency spending, mobilize more agencies, and establish temporary water systems as the area continues to grapple with its water supply crisis.

In a video posted Monday morning by the Butuan City Public Information Office, Fortun explained that the declaration was a necessary step to strengthen ongoing interventions and prepare the city for similar disruptions in the future.
The city council approved the declaration last Saturday through an urgent resolution after the water supply situation showed no significant improvement.
Fortun said the city government had already activated a task force in anticipation of the worsening crisis affecting the Butuan City Water District (BCWD) service areas.
He met with BCWD officials last Friday, which led to the deployment of additional water tankers, equipment, and logistical support for rationing and other emergency initiatives.
“We need to intensify our intervention,” Fortun said.
According to the mayor, the calamity declaration will allow immediate access to emergency funds to purchase more water tanks and rent pumps and generators, among others.

The calamity status will also enable a whole-of-government response, Fortun said, adding the water crisis should not be addressed solely by the city government and BCWD but must also involve national government agencies and others willing to help.

The declaration will also help the city intensify measures to protect public health, Fortun said, noting that prolonged water shortages can affect household sanitation, hygiene and access to safe drinking water.
Fortun said the city’s efforts would continue even after normal water service is restored.
The city government plans to establish more permanent or standby water supply systems in affected barangays to improve their readiness for future disruptions, he revealed.
Fortun said long-term solutions also include exploring alternative water sources outside of the Taguibo watershed.
The mayor acknowledged the frustration aired by residents affected by the water crisis, but appealed for patience, understanding, and cooperation while emergency measures are being implemented.
“This is not the time to quarrel. This is the time to work together as one community and one people of the city,” Fortun said./coa

articles.title: UK house prices fall for first time in nearly three years, says Lloyds
articles.summary: Average property cost £298,468 in August, down by 0.4% year on year owing to interest rates and uncertainty

blocks.text: UK house prices have fallen for the first time in almost three years, as prospective buyers were squeezed by higher mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty and stretched affordability.

Prices have dropped by 0.4% compared with a year ago, the first year-on-year decrease since November 2023, according to the lender Lloyds. That came in below expectations of a 0.2% annual rise, according to a poll of economists by Reuters.
The average property cost £298,468 in August, falling 0.2% or £685 compared with July, the bank’s monthly index found.
Andrew Asaam, a director at Lloyds, said the UK’s housing market was “subdued” in the face of higher inflation, borrowing costs and geopolitical tensions.

“What we’re not seeing is a rush of homeowners cutting prices,” he said. “But more are choosing to sit tight, with sellers reluctant to accept offers they feel are too low, while some buyers are waiting to see how conditions develop.”
He added that the market is forecast to “remain fairly subdued in the months ahead, but this will likely only have a limited impact on house prices”.
Tensions in the Middle East have stoked fears around inflation this year, feeding expectations of further interest rate rises.

Property buyers looking for a mortgage deal have faced months of heightened volatility, with the average rate for a two-year fixed residential mortgage at 5.6% on Friday, according to the market tracker Moneyfacts, while the average five-year deal was 5.66%. Both were below 5% at the start of the year.
Mortgage approvals were at their lowest level since the start of 2024, Lloyds said.

Jeremy Leaf, an estate agent in north London, said the slowdown in the market reflected a “standoff” between nervous buyers and sellers who believe they have already reduced their prices by as much as they can.
“There is more movement when sellers set realistic asking prices from the outset and appreciate after a period of marketing that even a cheeky offer is worth considering,” he said.
“Activity is picking up now that the main holiday season is over, which is helping to improve confidence a little.”
after newsletter promotion
Northern Ireland was still the best performer for house price growth across the UK, with the average home rising by 6.9% year on year to £231,245.
Prices in Scotland rose by 3.5% to an average of £223,437, while in Wales prices grew by 0.6% to an average of £230,282.
In England, there was a stark divide between the north and south, with the north-east and north-west recording growth of 2.7% and 2% respectively, with averages of £184,370 and £248,675.
Meanwhile the south-east reported the biggest drop in house prices across the UK, down by 1.6% to an average of £381,729. In greater London, prices dropped 1.5% to £534,177.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Anthony Codling said the Lloyds figures paint “a picture of a market under meaningful pressure from multiple directions: elevated mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty pushing up energy prices, and a consumer that is both cautious and increasingly stretched.
“Sellers are not panicking and cutting prices aggressively; they are simply sitting tight. Buyers, meanwhile, are waiting for clarity on the path of interest rates.”

articles.title: Jamaica to petition King Charles over slavery reparations
articles.summary: Jamaica will ask King Charles III to refer questions about the legality of slavery and Britain's potential obligation to provide reparations.

image.caption: The transatlantic slave trade between the 15th and 19th centuries involved the kidnapping, enslavement and transport of millions of Africans to the Americas and the Caribbean [FILE: April 11, 2026]Image: Raul Arboleda/AFP

blocks.text: The Jamaican government will petition King Charles III on Monday as the country seeks "reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement," the Culture Ministry said.

Culture Minister Olivia Grange is leading a delegation which will ask the king, Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the island's highest court of appeal in London.
The three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade are:

items: Whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law
Whether it broke international law, and
Whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress

blocks.text: Jamaica says the petition would be the first time a Commonwealth country has used the legal route to pursue reparatory justice.
What did Jamaica say about reparation for slavery?
Grange pointed to Britain's £20 million (€23.28 million) compensation payment to slave owners following the abolition of slavery in 1833.
"Up to 2015, Britain was paying the slave masters, because we were being considered property," Grange said.

"The question really should be: if in modern times we're still paying back the slave masters for the property that was our people, our ancestors, for property that was because of the abolition of slavery, then why shouldn't we be pursuing some remedy at this time?"
Grange said Jamaica wanted the legal questions answered before deciding on its next steps.
The Jamaican delegation will also meet British Museum officials to discuss the return of colonial-era artefacts.

blocks.caption: Grange said Jamaica wanted the legal questions answered before deciding on its next steps [FILE: July 22, 2025]Image: Randy Brooks/AFP

blocks.text: A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said the king has expressed his "commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs."
While Caribbean nations, in recent years have called for an apology and measures including debt relief, the British government has said it will not pay slavery reparations.
Transatlantic slave trade then and now

The transatlantic slave trade between the 15th and 19th centuries involved Europeans (and later Americans) kidnapping, enslaving and transporting of millions of Africans to their colonies in the Americas and the Caribbean.

An estimated 12–15 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic over four centuries, with about 10.7 million surviving the journey to the Americas. Up to 2 million died during the crossing.

Haiti gained independence from France in 1804 after a successful slave revolt, but France forced the new state in 1825 to pay 150 million gold francs to former slaveholders as compensation for "lost property," threatening war if it refused.
It took Haiti more than a hundred years to settle the debt plunging the Caribbean into a long-term cycle of poverty.

The legacy of slavery remains a contentious issue. Earlier in March, when the United Nations General Assembly voted to recognize the enslavement of Africans during the transatlantic slave trade as "the gravest crime against humanity," the United Kingdom and European Union member states abstained, while the United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the resolution.

SEOUL, South Korea – China could see recent cuts to US-South Korean military exercises as an opportunity to reassert itself in the Indo-Pacific, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said on Monday, September 7, though he said Washington had assured Manila that its commitments to the Philippines remained unchanged.

Speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of the Seoul Defense Dialogue, Teodoro said there had been no reduction in US-Philippine military activities and that bilateral and multilateral cooperation involving Manila continued to expand.

US President Donald Trump‘s decision last month to scale back military exercises with South Korea has prompted debate among security analysts over the credibility of US deterrence in Asia and whether rivals such as China could perceive a weakening of US resolve.
“It is a possibility, of course. China is very quick to exploit gaps,” Teodoro said when asked whether Beijing could seize on the move.
“If we’re talking about the Indo-Pacific as a whole, then it may signal some opportunity for China to reassert itself,” he said.

Teodoro said, however, that Manila had received “definite assurances” from Washington and that there was “no indication” that the changes in South Korea would affect commitments under the US-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty.

Manila has deepened defense cooperation with the United States under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., including expanded joint exercises and greater access for US forces to Philippine military facilities, as tensions with China have intensified in the South China Sea.

Teodoro said Manila was also broadening security ties with other partners. The Philippines recently concluded agreements with Canada and New Zealand, signed a visiting forces agreement with France, and was negotiating a similar pact with Britain, he said.
The defense chief also accused China of relying increasingly on influence operations alongside military and maritime pressure.
“Definitely it takes advantage of democratic space in order to co-opt people and to use a free media to expand its distortive narratives,” he said.
Teodoro said the Philippines was pursuing stronger espionage and foreign influence legislation to counter such activities.

Asked about Marcos’ recent remarks that progress was being made toward possible joint oil and gas exploration talks with China, Teodoro struck a cautious note, saying it would be “doubtful” that any economic cooperation could be insulated from longstanding sovereignty disputes in the South China Sea.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Manila did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Teodoro’s remarks.
Teodoro was in Seoul for talks aimed at expanding defense cooperation with South Korea, one of the Philippines’ largest arms suppliers.
South Korea has supplied the Philippines with FA-50 light combat aircraft, frigates and other military equipment as Manila modernises its armed forces.

He said the Philippines was interested in deeper industrial cooperation and emerging defense technologies from South Korea, but indicated that a long-discussed submarine acquisition program remained some way off.

“The submarine program is still under review,” he said, citing questions over mission requirements and the substantial infrastructure needed to support such a capability. “I would say it will be still a way off.”

Teodoro said concerns about China’s actions were encouraging closer security cooperation among countries across the region and could ultimately lead to a more interconnected Indo-Pacific security network.
“I believe so because the motivating factor there is China,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DOH steps up drive to address low vaccination coverage, hesitancy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday laid down its plans to intensify its campaign and measures to address low vaccination rates and vaccination hesitancy. During the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday laid down its plans to intensify its campaign and measures to address low vaccination rates and vaccination hesitancy.

During the continuation of the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the proposed budget of the DOH for next year, Rep. Girlie Veloso asked the agency for its concrete actions as she expressed her concern regarding the low vaccination coverage among children aged 12 to 23 months.
Citing the 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey, she noted that 4 out of 10 children among this age group were not fully vaccinated.

DOH Undersecretary Gloria Balboa acknowledged that the agency needs to “sustain and increase public trust” as she shared that one of the reasons behind the low vaccination rate, aside from delays in vaccine procurement, is the “persistent vaccine hesitancy that is brought about by, let’s say, misinformation.”
Balboa underscored the importance of coordinating with local government officials and other authorities to help address vaccine hesitancy among communities by strengthening information campaigns.

“We have to involve our community leaders, those people that they trust in the community para magtiwala yung ating mga magulang para magpabakuna and improve on our information campaign kasi we really need to do this, medyo matagal na po but then still there is a need to intensify, educate our parents and all the members of the community,” she said.

(We have to involve our community leaders, those people that they trust in the community so the parents can trust us to vaccinate their children and improve on our information campaign because we really need to do this, this has been overdue but then still there is a need to intensify, educate our parents and all the members of the community.)
Aside from these measures, Balboa said the DOH will have to strengthen its vaccine supply and cold chain management system, as well as disease surveillance and outbreak response.
In the same hearing, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said early procurement of vaccines for the agency’s immunization programs has been set.

He noted that some vaccines are delivered depending on their seasonality, such as flu and pneumonia vaccines, and the calendar of schools, such as human papillomavirus and cervical cancer vaccines for school girls.
Lastly, Balboa said that there is a need to digitalize the immunization information system.

“This is part of the digitalization that our present leadership will look into para mas maayos po yung ating information that we get especially on the ground that will guide us in our policy and decision making,” Balboa added.
(This is part of the digitalization that our present leadership will look into so we can get proper information especially on the ground that will guide us in our policy and decision making.) /gsg

articles.title: DepEd can’t hire new teachers in 2027 due to budget cuts – Angara
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will not be able to hire new public school teachers next year after its recruitment program was left unfunded in the agency’s proposed…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will not be able to hire new public school teachers next year after its recruitment program was left unfunded in the agency’s proposed budget, its secretary, Sonny Angara, said on Monday.
Asked at a congressional budget hearing if funding for hiring new teachers in 2027 had been zeroed out, Angara said: “Yes.”
“Unfortunately, there was none,” he told lawmakers in mixed English and Filipino. “But we’re hoping that it will be hiked in the course of the budgetary process.”
DepEd was earmarked P973.40 billion under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, 3.87 percent lower than its P1.01-trillion funding this year.

Angara’s presentation to lawmakers showed that the agency had requested an additional P49.16 billion for its “personnel improvement” program, including P4.29 billion for the hiring of 14,274 teachers.
“This is part of the wish list,” he said.

His appeal comes as legislators review the P7.2-trillion spending plan. Congress is the final arbiter and can cut or tweak funding at its discretion, leaving the door open for amendments to DepEd’s budget proposal.
Angara said DepEd hires an average of 20,000 teachers a year, noting that the agency received enough funding to hire 32,000 teachers for 2026.
“We got 32,000 this year, which is above the average hiring [average],” he said.
Besides funding for Teacher I posts, Angara also requested P16.64 billion for hiring 39,428 Project Development Officer I staff and P10.52 billion to fund 14,126 School Principal I posts. /mcm

articles.title: Adult dugong found dead off Antique town
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY — A day after residents of an Antique island helped a stranded juvenile dugong return to the sea, another of the threatened marine mammals was found dead along the coast of the province.…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY — A day after residents of an Antique island helped a stranded juvenile dugong return to the sea, another of the threatened marine mammals was found dead along the coast of the province.
The dugong, or sea cow (Dugong dugon), was discovered along the shoreline of Barangay Aras-Asan in Sebaste town on Monday morning.
Authorities responded to the area and examined the carcass to help determine the possible cause of death and arrange its proper handling.
Flord Nicson Calawag, a licensed fisheries technologist and biodiversity researcher, said the animal appeared to be a large adult based on photographs of the carcass.

“From these photos, the dugong appears to be a large adult species. There are some superficial marks and abrasions visible on the body, but the photographs alone cannot establish the cause of death,” Calawag said.
He said the prevailing southwest monsoon, locally known as habagat, could have brought the carcass to the shoreline.
“There is a strong possibility that the adult dugong was washed ashore by strong waves associated with the prevailing Habagat in Antique,” Calawag said.

blocks.caption: Adult dugong found dead off Antique waters

blocks.text: But he stressed that being washed ashore would not explain what caused the animal to die in the first place.

“A proper examination or necropsy is necessary to establish the cause of death and determine whether it may be linked to fishing activities, ingestion of marine debris, vessel collision, disease or other natural or human-related factors,” he said.
Authorities had yet to announce the results of an examination or determine when and how the dugong died.
The discovery came just a day after a juvenile dugong became stranded during low tide on Liwagao Island in Barangay Sibolo, Caluya town, also in Antique.
Residents came to the juvenile’s aid and successfully helped it return to the sea on Sept. 6.

No indication suggested the two incidents were related. But their occurrence on successive days drew attention to dugongs’ presence in Antique waters and concerns about protecting the species and its coastal habitat.

Dugongs are herbivorous marine mammals that depend largely on seagrass meadows in shallow coastal waters. They reproduce slowly, making the loss of breeding adults particularly significant to small or declining populations.
Based on documentation, dugongs are threatened by accidental capture and entanglement in fishing gear, vessel strikes, hunting, and the degradation or loss of seagrass habitat.
Calawag cautioned, however, that none of these possible causes could be attributed to the Sebaste dugong without a proper examination of the carcass./coa

articles.title: Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
articles.summary: The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died. Almost half of people infected with Ebola…

blocks.text: The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died.

Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet, the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%.
But often, it’s because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself.
“Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research,” the aid organization wrote in early September.

At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak.

But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms.

Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won’t be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children.

According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak.

For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff.
Ebola in Berlin

In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin’s Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134.
“Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out,” said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments.
The available data about the drug’s impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father.

In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It’s unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can’t be mapped onto the larger population either.

But the test was valuable nonetheless. “The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build,” Le said.
Why do such gaps in knowledge exist?
Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as “small adults.”

Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women.

That’s why dosages of medication can’t simply be transferred from adults to children. It’s also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example.

“All of this creates extra costs,” said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority.

“It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults,” said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. “That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women.”
Biot said it’s sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. “Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children,” he argued.
A difficult balance

None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide.
This isn’t an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed.

Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn’t made for children. The WHO advised it be used “off label” for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they’ve observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

blocks.caption: When it comes to the development of medicines and vaccines, the first samples are often made for adult patients Image: Thomas Lohnes/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “When you’re doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product,” said Russell. “But when you’re in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes.”

Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. “They shouldn’t be excluded from participation just like that,” she said. “Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset.”

Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress.
“No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products,” he said. /dl

MANILA, Philippines – A top official of the Philippine Statistics Authority told the impeachment court on Monday, September 7, that the signatories of the confidential fund receipts of Vice President Sara Duterte‘s offices bore the names of children and dead people.

According to Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande, out of 2,669 alleged confidential fund payees of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd), only 152 had a single-matched entry in the PSA’s civil registry system.
From that number, 37 had death records, such as the names Fortunato Salig, Emilio Sagan, Rodolfo Traya, and Marlin Sunga.
Twenty-five names, meanwhile, have birthdays that indicate they are under 16 years old, such as Beatrice Cuenca, Miko Aluizar, and Mikay delos Reyes.
In total, 1,685 names have no PSA certificates of live birth, marriage, or death.
“In short, confidential funds were liquidated in the names of the non-existent, the long dead, and children,” prosecutor Mae Divinagracia said in her offer of testimony.

blocks.caption: PSA: Some OVP, DepEd confidential fund recipients had names of kids, dead people

blocks.text: The non-existent records include that of “Mary Grace Piattos,” the infamous name flagged during the House’s investigation against Duterte’s confidential spending in 2024. The name appears to be a combination of a restaurant chain and a snack brand.
Piattos was originally part of the witness list of the prosecution, but the team said it will no longer present her.
“What’s important is that according to PSA records, she doesn’t exist. It’s difficult to find someone who does not exist,” prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong said.

blocks.caption: PSA: Some OVP, DepEd confidential fund recipients had names of kids, dead people

blocks.text: Defending the Vice President, her lawyer Justin Gular argued that not all births, marriage, and deaths are recorded in the PSA’s database, and that the PSA does not have a repository of aliases used in confidential operations.
Duterte’s camp also claimed for the first time that the names were aliases.

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo said the use of aliases in government agencies such as the Philippine National Police and the National Bureau of Investigation is a standard operating procedure but he flagged the possibility that only one person signed the receipts due to similar handwriting. – Rappler.com

Malacañang on Monday said government security agencies have no record of threats against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the Philippine National Police (PNP) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) had no reports, complaints, or records indicating a threat to Duterte’s life.

She said government agencies tasked with providing security continue to protect all Filipinos, including Duterte.
Castro challenged the Vice President to provide evidence to support her claim that she is not safe.

“Patungkol sa sinasabing atake ni Pangulong Marcos Jr. sa kaniya personal, 2024 pa. Hindi po ito nabanggit ninuman o nabanggit man lang niya noong panahon na sinasabing siya ay inaatake noong 2024 pa. Wala rin po siya nabanggit patungkol sa sinasabing threats way back 2023,” she said.

(Regarding the alleged attack by President Marcos Jr. on her personally, back in 2024. No one mentioned this or she did not mention this at the time when she was allegedly being attacked back in 2024. She also did not mention anything about the alleged threats way back in 2023.)

articles.title: DepEd seeks P9.98B for ARAL after zero allocation in 2027 budget
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) is asking Congress for P9.98 billion to fund its Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) program in the proposed 2027 national budget after the National…

blocks.text: Published September 7, 2026 2:23pm

The Department of Education (DepEd) is asking Congress for P9.98 billion to fund its Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) program in the proposed 2027 national budget after the National Expenditure Program (NEP) allocated no funds for the initiative, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said Monday.

During the agency’s budget hearing at the House of Representatives, Angara asked lawmakers to provide funding for the program as he defended DepEd’s proposed P975.96-billion budget for 2027, including allocations for its attached agencies.

“Regarding the ARAL program, there is zero allotment for this under the 2027 budget, unlike this year when there was an allotment of around P9 billion for the different aspects of the ARAL,” Angara said.
The request includes funding for ARAL tutors, learning recovery and remediation consultations, summer program tutors, external tutors, learning resources, tutor orientation and program management.
Angara said P1.09 billion of the request would cover compensation for 15,800 ARAL tutors, while P3.5 billion in total is being sought for the remuneration of ARAL teachers and tutors.
He said DepEd considers the program effective, citing results among the 6.7 million learners who participated in it.

“Our program has achieved good results because among the 6.7 million learners who participated in the ARAL program, we found at the end of the school year that 4.5 million had been struggling readers, while 2.5 million improved to grade-level reading. So they are now reading at the right level,” he said.
Bulacan 6th District Rep. Salvador Pleyto III, meanwhile, called for adequate funding for the program, particularly to ensure that teachers serving as ARAL tutors are properly compensated.
“If we are asking them to provide additional tutoring beyond their regular responsibilities, we must ensure that they are properly and fairly compensated,” Pleyto said.
Angara assured lawmakers that compensation for ARAL teachers and tutors was included in DepEd’s budget request.
“The remuneration of ARAL teachers and tutors is included in our request, Your Honor. We are requesting a total of P3.5 billion for their remuneration. It is already included,” he said.
Angara said the proposed P975.96-billion budget aims to further expand and strengthen programs, services and guidance for students, teachers and schools nationwide.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 270,000 stranded as airports extend closure
articles.summary: Anak Krakatau, which lies about 150km from the capital Jakarta, began erupting late on Friday.

blocks.text: Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.
Finna, who was supposed to fly home to Jakarta from Malang, a city in East Java, on Sunday morning, described the frezny at the airport as flights got repeatedly rescheduled.
"It was very crowded because passengers from the morning flights had piled up, while those scheduled for later departures still didn't know what would happen," the 46-year-old told BBC Indonesian.
"We were all glued to the flight information screens."
Not wanting to deal with the uncertainty, Finna eventually spent the night on two intercity trains before arriving in Jakarta at 03:00 on Monday.

"Everyone seems to be racking their brains [figuring alternative transportation options]", said Jo Shaw, who was visiting Indonesia with members of her conservation charity Save the Rhino International.
Shaw's team had axed their plans to camp out at Java's Ujung Kulon National Park after authorities raised its alert level for the Anak Krakatau volcano.

"Being stranded in an airport hotel is a relatively minor inconvenience to be resolved in a few days hopefully," Shaw said, adding that she was more concerned about the teams working on the ground with the rhinos under such environmental conditions.
A newly wed Malaysian couple who had just spent a week in Bali said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September.

"What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama.
"We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said.
On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high".
Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said.
Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency.
"We ‌cannot ascertain when this ‌will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports.
Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding".

Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it.
Authorities have also confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano.

Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.
Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.

The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.
Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.
With reporting by Farida Susanty in Jakarta and Koh Ewe in Singapore

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo appeals for Lachica, Nolasco testimony in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Senator-Judge Raffy Tulfo on Monday said security officers Colonel Raymund Lachica and Colonel Dennis Nolasco should still be called as witnesses in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published September 7, 2026 2:01pm

Senator-Judge Raffy Tulfo on Monday said security officers Colonel Raymund Lachica and Colonel Dennis Nolasco should still be called as witnesses in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte to give answers on the unusual names indicated on the acknowledgement receipts of the confidential funds.

On the 22nd day of the trial, Tulfo made the manifestation as Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande testified that some confidential fund payees listed by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd) have no birth, marriage, and death records.

“For me it's really important na mapatawag dito ‘yung Lachica at saka ‘yung counterpart ni Lachica sa DepEd para sila talaga ang may kinalaman doon sa pagbibigay ng mga pangalan na ‘yan,” the senator-judge said.
(For me it's really important to call Lachica and his counterpart at DepEd as they are the ones who are really involved in giving those names.)
“I’m very sure, Mr. Presiding Officer, habang pini-fill up-an nila ang mga pangalan, nagtatawanan ‘yun, ginagawa tayong mga kengkoy, ‘yung mga tao diyan sa DepEd at saka tao diyan sa OVP,” he added.
(I'm very sure, Mr. Presiding Officer, while they were filling up the names, the people at DepEd and OVP were laughing at it, making fun of us.)
Tulfo also expressed belief that the unusual names listed were only aliases.
Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia, however, pointed out that the defense never claimed anything regarding the use of aliases.

“If such was the fact, Your Honor, then the defense should have at the earliest opportunity already indicated that in their answer. But they never did, Your Honor. So we worked on the theory that these are the real names of the supposed payees,” Divinagracia said.
Defense counsel Justin Gular, in response, said that in relation to the Article 1 of the impeachment case, the basis of the prosecution was the findings of the Commission on Audit (COA).

“The findings of the Commission on Audit never pointed any problems in relation to the names in the acknowledgment receipts, much less the use of aliases. There was nothing to respond to, with all due respect,” Gular said.
The House prosecbe ution panel announced last Friday, September 5, that it would no longer presenting Lachica and Nolasco, as well as Ramil Madriaga, as witnesses in the impeachment trial.

Lachica and Nolasco served as chief and deputy chief of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group, respectively. They allegedly disbursed the confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, then concurrently headed by Duterte.

articles.title: Remulla wary that Duterte ‘would punch’ cops if arrested
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla has revealed that they were concerned that Vice President Sara Duterte’s possible arrest for grave threats may lead to her punching…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla has revealed that they were concerned that Vice President Sara Duterte’s possible arrest for grave threats may lead to her punching police officers enforcing the order.

In a press briefing in Camp Crame on Monday, Remulla noted that Philippine National Police–Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP–CIDG) personnel had coordinated with Duterte’s camp regarding the warrant to arrest her for grave threats.
The Secretary said he was not worried that Duterte’s supporters would launch protests to defend her if she was arrested.
“We weren’t worried about that. We were more worried baka manuntok siya ng nagse-serve ng warrant,” he said.
(We weren’t worried about that. We were more worried that she would punch an officer serving the arrest warrant.)
Remulla was referring to a 2011 incident in which Duterte punched a court sheriff for supposedly disregarding her plea to stop the demolition of houses in a contested parcel of land in Davao City.
“We didn’t want that to happen. She has a predilection for violence. And she has a predilection for extreme efforts to get her way,” Remulla said.
“Ayaw ko namang may masuntok kaming CIDG ng vice president, so we treated her with all the necessary courtesy na benefitted ng being vice president,” he added.
(I didn’t want CIDG personnel to be punched by the vice president, so we treated her with all the necessary courtesy that she benefits from being vice president.)
The Inquirer sought comment from Duterte’s legal counsel, Michael Poa and Paul Lawrence Lim, but they have yet to respond as of this writing.
On Friday, Duterte was ordered arrested by the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for three counts of grave threats.

The charges were in connection with alleged threats she made during a November 2024 virtual press conference against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then-House Speaker and presidential cousin Martin Romualdez.
Earlier in the briefing, Remulla said that CIDG personnel attempted to serve the warrant on Duterte at her home in San Juan City and her office in Mandaluyong City.
But authorities did not arrest her, and she did not post bail until Saturday./coa

articles.title: Tiny cash buffers leave small UK TV firms at risk of going bust, analysis finds
articles.summary:
Median £42,000 in reserve not enough to cover filming overrun or delay to series, industry body warns

Hundreds of small UK TV companies have so little cash in reserve that a filming overrun…

blocks.text: Hundreds of small UK TV companies have so little cash in reserve that a filming overrun or a delay to a series could send them bust, an industry body has warned, as programme budget cuts by broadcasters threaten their future.

Analysis of the Companies House accounts filings of more than 200 of the estimated 800 independent TV production companies in the UK by the industry body Indielab has found that 40% face running out of cash within the next two years.

The analysis of three years of filings made by small independent TV producers, the “indies” that make up 85% of the UK’s production sector, identified a dramatic drain on the financial reserves they use to weather tough trading periods.
The reserves of more than half declined over the three-year period, with 40% registering a decline of almost a third, while the financial cushion for 31% was slashed by more than half.
The analysis found that the amount held in reserves by a typical small indie – the median amount of the sample of 203 – was only £42,000 at the end of the three-year analysis period.
The comparable figure at the beginning of the period was £51,000, already a slim reserve fund to rely on to bridge funding shortages.

“[The £42,000] buffer would not cover the cost of a single delayed commission, a production overrun, or a series put on hold [by a broadcaster] after delivery,” said Victoria Powell, the chief executive of Indielab. “The picture is stark. Small producers are the most exposed part of the ecosystem. When commissioning spend falls, they feel it first and hardest. Our data shows the sector’s health is being eroded, year on year.”
A string of high-profile TV production companies have already been wound down in the past two years.

blocks.caption: Duck Soup Films, which made the drama Lost Boys & Fairies for the BBC, has stopped active development and production. Photograph: Simon Ridgway/BBC/Duck Soup Films

blocks.text: These include Euston Films, the maker of the pre-apocalyptic thriller Hard Sun and the train drama Nightsleeper for the BBC, and Dare Pictures, which has produced Channel 4 shows including Fugitive: The Mystery of the Crypto Queen and UK Prisons Exposed: Sex, Drugs & Corruption.

Other notable production closures include Leeds-based Duck Soup Films, which made the drama Lost Boys & Fairies for the BBC and Channel 4’s Dreamers, and the factual producer Proper Content, which had credits including the BBC documentary P Diddy: The Rise and Fall, the Channel 5 royal docuseries The King’s Guard and the Channel 4 show The School That Tried To End Racism.

“We have seen many notable closures across the sector in the last two years,” Powell said. “We know of many more companies that have quietly closed or mothballed outside the headlines. Our data strongly suggests this trend will accelerate.”

Last week, Everyone TV, the joint venture owned by the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5, released a report that warned of a “spiral of decline” affecting the production industry if broadcaster budgets continued to be cut.
Despite the arrival of the deep-pocketed US streamers such as Netflix, Amazon and Disney+, the UK production industry still relies heavily on traditional UK broadcasters for their livelihood.
after newsletter promotion

The report, by Oliver & Ohlbaum, found that public service broadcasters (PSBs) remain the leading source of UK original commissions and production for small indies, accounting for 71% of UK original content investment in 2024 and 85% of all original hours last year.

However, the total amount spent on commissioning programmes by all UK-based broadcasters has fallen from £1.99bn in 2022 to £1.73bn in 2024 – the lowest level since the industry shut down during the Covid pandemic in 2020 – according to the most recent figures from the industry body Pact.
This fall has mainly been because of significant decreases by multichannel broadcasters, such as Sky, where spend has declined by almost 40% over that period.

Figures from the British Film Institute showed that spending on prestige shows – high-end TV costing at least £1m an hour to make – by domestic broadcasters has declined from £794m in 2023 to £688m last year.

“PSBs with a statutory duty to support independent production need to consider what that duty really means in practice, and whether they are currently meeting it,” Powell said. “The accounts of 203 indie TV companies should be a wake-up call to the sector.”
Indielab’s research focused on small indies with a turnover of less than £10m.
Pact, which represents the wider industry, says it has 800 independent production company members, the majority of which are small and medium-sized with a turnover of less than £50m.

articles.title: Ministers propose converting female prison estate into cells for men
articles.summary:
Plans would see parts of estate converted but campaigners warn it just ‘moves the crisis from one part to another’

Ministers will seriously examine converting parts of the female prison…

blocks.text: Ministers will seriously examine converting parts of the female prison estate into cells that can safely house male prisoners, as the government looks to reduce numbers of women in prison to ease strain on the system.

The prisons minister Catherine McKinnell is to look into the practicalities of converting female spaces to male over the coming months, after warnings from governors and experts that it would pose significant challenges.

Andy Burnham said earlier in the summer that the government was keen to examine freeing more women from prison as a way of building capacity in the system to avoid the early release of more dangerous male prisoners.

But in the details released this week on ways the government planned to free up more space, the emphasis was on deporting foreign offenders and reducing the number of prisoners serving highly controversial imprisonment for public protection sentences, which keep people inside for an indefinite spell.

After a backlash from victims and families, Burnham changed plans for the early release of some prisoners as part of a plan to ease overcrowding. He said he would be preventing the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.

About 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early in 10 tranches from October under the plans, 1,500 fewer than before Burnham’s interventions. Experts including the former justice secretary David Gauke have warned that the government is taking a big risk running prisons so close to capacity.

But the Guardian understands that officials have told ministers that plans to reduce the number of female prisoners will need much longer-term planning. Andrea Coomber, chief executive of penal reform charity the Howard League, said a genuine reduction in the number of female prisoners would be welcome, but not simply happen to free up space for men.

“[It] does nothing to fix a prison system that is fundamentally too full – it just moves the crisis from one part of the estate to another,” she said. “Without real investment in women’s centres and community alternatives, women risk being sacrificed to the scramble for more beds for men.”

Women currently represent less than 5% of the total prison population in Britain, with 12 dedicated jails. Government sources also said those who would be more likely to be freed would be those on mother and baby units where they cannot be replaced by male prisoners.

The victims minister Alex Davies-Jones said the government still believed that the “vast majority of women who are in prison, many of whom are mothers and have young children, shouldn’t necessarily be there. They are victims in their own right, and they can be appropriately managed in the community through women’s centres.”

But she said that the government could not take a “one-size-fits-all approach” to converting female prisons into male spaces, telling LBC: “There are some women who absolutely should be in prison, and they will remain there.

“But where there is a case to answer that we can re-purpose the female estate, because we know the prison capacity problem is in our male estate, 98% at capacity in the male estate, then we will look to re-purpose to see what we can do to free up capacity and move the estates around.”

Pia Sinha, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said a smaller women’s prison estate could be a positive step if it reduced the number of women jailed and increased the support in communities, who had complex and often unmet needs.

“Any decision about the future of the women’s estate must recognise this reality,” she said. “Rather than viewing a women’s prison as a solution to overcrowding in the men’s estate, the government’s priority should be implementing the Women’s Justice Board’s recommendations and building the community support that can deliver better outcomes for women and safely reduce the number of women in custody in the first place.”
