blocks.text: MIAMI, United States — At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.

Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centers “in critical condition” and two more were treated at a local hospital.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” which left “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles,” Jadallah said.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team” was needed, “including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 that had arrived around 2 pm (1800 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the “crash,” fire officials said.
“A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting,” Jadallah said.
“The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB,” he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.

The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have “launched a go team to investigate Sunday’s runway excursion accident.”

The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travelers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.
Amazon put out a statement saying the aircraft “experienced an incident while attempting to land.” It did not say if anyone was hurt or killed.

“This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in the statement.
Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a “really tragic scene,” but there was “no apparent threat to public safety.” /dl

articles.title: ICC chief Akane vows to continue job no matter what amid US sanctions
articles.summary: Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court, vowed on Sunday that she will continue to do her job, despite the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump imposing sanctions on her…

blocks.text: Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court, vowed on Sunday that she will continue to do her job, despite the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump imposing sanctions on her and other officials of the Hague-based judicial body.

“No matter what happens, my convictions will not waver. I will continue to conduct investigations, prosecutions and judicial proceedings as I have until now,” she said, appearing online at an event in Tokyo.
She is among the ICC judges targeted by U.S. sanctions that freeze assets in the United States, with Washington accusing the ICC of encroaching on state sovereignty.
Akane, the first Japanese national to head the ICC, described the punitive measures as a threat to judges and to the principle of neutrality.
Speaking about the threat to the rule of law from the sanctions, Akane said, “Silence is tantamount to accepting rule by overwhelming pressure or force,” adding, “I will not give up.”
The Trump administration has strongly objected to ICC probes into alleged war crimes committed by U.S. military personnel.
Akane also urged Japan to take a proactive role in efforts to cooperate with many countries and prosecute serious crimes, calling on it to “actively join the global effort now.”

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has said the sanctions were “incompatible” with her country’s commitment to the rule of law, after initially coming under scrutiny over her initial remarks that the measures were “very unfortunate,” in language seen as stopping short of criticizing Japan’s sole treaty ally.
On Friday, Gen Nakatani, a former defense minister who leads a nonpartisan parliamentary group advocating human rights diplomacy, called on Takaichi to urge Washington to retract the sanctions.
“Upholding the Japan-U.S. alliance and defending the rule of law is not a choice between two options,” he said.
A former prosecutor, Akane became president of the ICC in March 2024. Japan is the largest financial contributor to the court. /dl

articles.title: Germany’s far-right AfD thanks Elon Musk as France warns state election win a ‘serious moment’
articles.summary:
Lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt welcomes further ‘strong’ cooperation with Musk as French minister says ‘We cannot forget our history’

The candidate who led the far-right Alternative für…

blocks.text: The candidate who led the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party to a historic state election victory in Germany has thanked Elon Musk for his support, as one French minister warned that this was a “serious moment” for Europe.

The AfD more than doubled its support in the Saxony-Anhalt region and appears to be on the brink of becoming the first far-right party to gain power in Germany at state level since the second world war.

On Sunday night, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X “for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time”, adding: “I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation”.
Siegmund wrote his comments after Musk said “Well done!” in German to AfD co-founder Alice Weidel, when she posted about the projected win.

Earlier, US president Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the election projection without comment on his Truth Social site. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.

Exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.4% of the vote, a larger share than predicted, and decisively larger than that of the Christian Democrats (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world. However, it still remains unclear as to how and whether the AfD will be able to form a government, having ruled out entering a coalition and being refused any form of cooperation by the mainstream parties.
The CDU was trailing massively on around 18.4% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.3%, with the Social Democrats on 8.4% and the Greens on 8.7% by around early evening.
France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, described the win as “a serious moment in Europe”, warning that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be a solution”.
“We must listen with humility to the anger, the concerns, the fears, and respond to them,” he added. “We cannot forget our history. That is the meaning behind the choices made by France and Germany.”
Donald Tusk, the prime minister of Poland, said: “In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany.”

The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.

Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Indonesia volcano eruption: 8 airports shut, 170,000 passengers affected
articles.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — A volcano erupted in Indonesia early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic…

blocks.text: JAKARTA, Indonesia — A volcano erupted in Indonesia early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports as ash drifted across western parts of the country.

The volcanic island of Anak Krakatau, located in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands, had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m. Sunday and for 16 seconds about three hours later, Indonesia’s Geological Agency said. Closed-circuit camera footage showed lava flares from the volcano.

No casualties were reported and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the active crater.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra’s southern tip, Indonesia’s Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.

AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as six other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
Flights canceled as 170,000 passengers affected

By Sunday evening, the closure of eight airports had affected 170,000 passengers from 1,558 canceled flights, including 963 flights in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport alone. All eight airports were ordered closed until 8:59 a.m. Monday.
“It’s of course an inconvenience,” said Diego Urdiales, a Spanish tourist who was supposed to fly home to Madrid. “I was supposed to get input from the airline … but so far no news.”
“It’s a natural disaster, it’s a force majeure, so, what can we do?” said Michele Gouw, an Indonesian passenger. “We just have to accept it and wait for the airline and airport directions.”

Indonesia’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation said that it was closely monitoring the eruption’s impact on air travel and coordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency.
“Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The eruption also disrupted services at Bali’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport and at Medan.
Volcano remains active
Indonesia’s volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery.

One plume rose to 20,000 feet (6,100 meters) and drifted northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters. A second cloud reached 50,000 feet (15,200 meters) and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.
Lana Saria, head of Indonesia’s Geological Agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has intensified since July, with Sunday’s eruption the strongest during that period.
The repeated eruptions indicate a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases beneath the volcano, she said, though officials can’t predict whether a larger eruption will occur.
“We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” Saria said in a video briefing.
She said the main hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas and the ejection of hot rocks and other material around the crater area.
Schools move to online learning

The eruption’s impact extended beyond air travel. The government on Sunday authorized schools in areas affected by volcanic ash could temporarily move to online learning at home. The measure is intended to reduce students’ exposure to ashfall and allow local authorities to adjust classroom activities based on conditions on the ground.
Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau,” is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.

An eruption of Anak Krakatau in 2018 caused a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau’s southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Scientists said that Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption. /dl

articles.title: Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
articles.summary: Five people are dead and five seriously injured after a Boeing 767-300 cargo plane "overran" the runway and caught fire, officials say.

blocks.text: An Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five more.

The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft crashed just before 14:00 local time (19:00 GMT) after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The flight also hit several vehicles on the ground.
Amazon said that it is "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened".

All flights were ordered grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as fire crews raced to the smoking crash site. The crash comes over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year.
"At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured," Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening.
She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within "seconds" of the crash.
"Right now, our focus is on the families, those who were injured, and the ongoing response," she continued.
Three of the five people injured are in critical condition, said Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah. The mayor said they were all taken to hospital with "unknown injuries".
Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, said Jadallah.

Officials say it is too early to know the cause of the crash, and that it will be investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board. The federal agency, which investigates all air crashes in the US, plans to hold a news conference on Monday.

The Amazon flight operated by 21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, "overran Miami International Airport's diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport," the airport said in a statement.
Miami Dade Fire Rescue said crews "arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing".
The BBC has emailed 21 Air about the incident, but has not received a response.
Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows that the Amazon cargo flight was travelling at 112 knots (129mph, 207km/h) as it exited the "useable runway".
In a blog post, the site says the plane came to rest near a parking lot that services an Amazon warehouse and other businesses.
There were light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami at the time of the incident, the site says.
The crash comes during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year in the US.
The Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) predicted 17 million travellers at US airports in the week leading up to Monday's Labor Day holiday.
The TSA, which screens passengers flying in the US, predicted that 2.3 million people would fly on Sunday alone.

articles.title: China state media revives 'manufactured' Batanes claim
articles.summary: Chinese state media again questioned Philippine sovereignty over its northernmost province.

blocks.text: September 7, 2026 | 8:20am

The Tao (Yami) indigenous rowers paddle a traditional wooden canoe called Ovayan (Golden Friendship) during its voyage to Philippines' Batanes Islands, along the coastline at Orchid island (or Lanyu island), southeastern Taiwan on June 15, 2026.
AFP / Cheng Yu-chen

MANILA, Philippines — Chinese state media has again amplified claims questioning Philippine sovereignty over Batanes, publishing an opinion piece that argues Manila has no legal basis for exercising jurisdiction over the country's northernmost province.

The September 3 article in the state-run Global Times comes two months after scholars from several Chinese institutions first advanced the claim that Batanes belongs to China through Taiwan. Beijing, however, has not formally asserted sovereignty over the province.

The opinion piece, titled "History shows that Batanes Islands do not belong to the Philippines," was written by Wang Yuanyuan, an assistant research fellow at the Center for South China Sea History and Culture of China's National Institute for South China Sea Studies.
Wang argued that Batanes historically fell outside Philippine territorial boundaries and was instead linked to Taiwan, questioning the legal basis for Philippine sovereignty over the islands.
Manila-based think tank Stratbase Institute rejected the renewed assertion, describing its repetition as a "clear attempt to manufacture ambiguity where none exists."
"Batanes is Philippine territory, its people are Filipinos, and its sovereignty is settled and not up for debate," Victor Andres "Dindo" Manhit, president of Stratbase, said.

He urged the Philippine government to mount a sustained response through diplomacy, law, public information and governance to prevent repeated assertions from developing into what he described as a "manufactured dispute."
"An opinion piece cannot rewrite history, international agreements, or more than two centuries of continuous Philippine administration," Manhit said.
Earlier claims

The latest Global Times article follows a June 30 symposium at Jinan University in Guangzhou, where scholars from Chinese universities and research institutions argued that Batanes was a "natural geographical extension" of Taiwan and that sovereignty therefore belonged to China.
Participants included scholars from Jinan University, Nanjing University, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and other institutions.
Global Times published the arguments in July, reporting that some of the scholars called on China to take action to assert sovereignty over Batanes.
The claims drew strong objections from Philippine officials.
The Department of Foreign Affairs said Philippine sovereignty over Batanes was "settled and not up for debate" and rejected what it called revisionist claims over Philippine territory.

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines also disputed the scholars' historical arguments. It said Philippine governments and their legal predecessors have continuously administered Batanes since Spain formally incorporated the islands into the Province of Cagayan in 1783.
The NHCP also said historical records did not support claims that Batanes was governed as part of Taiwan during the Ming or Qing dynasties.

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. separately dismissed the assertions as baseless, while Batanes Rep. Ciriaco Gato Jr. stressed that the province and the Ivatan people are unequivocally Filipino.

articles.title: Susan Sarandon says she is losing movie roles because of her support for Palestine
articles.summary:
Oscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studios

The Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon has said she is still…

blocks.text: The Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon has said she is still losing work because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, despite what she ⁠described as a broader shift ⁠in public opinion against ​US support for Israel.
Speaking at the Venice film festival, where she is promoting her latest movie The Echo Chamber, Sarandon said some parts of the film industry continued to ⁠shun her over her activism.

“I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics,” ⁠she said. “That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really ​understood that.“
US opinion polls have shown support ‌for Israel softening and sympathy for ‌Palestinians rising since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.
But the 79-year-old actor said her support for the Palestinian ‌cause continued to carry professional consequences.

“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she told reporters. “But that’s the power structure. I think [among] people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome.“
An Academy Award winner for Dead Man Walking, Sarandon rose to prominence in films including The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Bull Durham and Thelma and Louise.

She was dropped by her longstanding talent agency UTA in 2023 after ‌remarks she made while attending pro-Palestinian rallies one month after the Hamas attack on Israel, including: “There are a lot of people afraid of being Jewish at this time, and are getting a taste of what it feels like to be a Muslim in this country.”
The conflict has spilled into this year’s Venice film festival, with activists ​calling on organisers to raise the Palestinian flag in recognition of Palestinian directors screening at the event.

The festival’s artistic director, Alberto Barbera, has said this is impossible because Italy does not formally recognise the state of Palestine, but he has pointed to several films being shown on the Lido that show the struggle of ordinary Palestinians.
Sarandon said resistance to hiring outspoken critics of Israel ⁠remained particularly strong among major studios.

“If it is a major studio, I think ​it’s not just with me but with ​other people who have been told ​that that is impossible,” she said, thanking Andrea Pallaoro, the director of The Echo Chamber, for casting ​her.
“I found my family, ‌I found my people ​and I’m OK,” she ​said, sparking prolonged applause at the news conference.

In her latest film, adapted from the final screenplay by Italian film-maker Bernardo Bertolucci, Sarandon plays an ageing singer who hires a music producer recovering from drug addiction to work on a comeback album.
The Echo Chamber is one of 21 films competing for Venice’s Golden Lion award, which will be presented on 12 September.

articles.title: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
articles.summary: The government says the law is intended to protect the rights of young girls, but critics say it is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling.

blocks.text: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.
The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country.
Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood".
But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional.

The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls.
Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban".
"We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said.
"Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support."

The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court.
The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality.
Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians.
If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685).
Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban.
The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers".
She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties.

The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike.
The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools".

Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state".
In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years.
The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women.
Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public.
Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups."
"Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.

articles.title: Heavy habagat rain threatens floods in 4 Luzon provinces
articles.summary: Metro Manila may see scattered rain and thunderstorms Monday as southwest monsoon rains linger.

blocks.text: September 7, 2026 | 7:34am
PAGASA tracks Tropical Storm Krovanh 1,145 kilometers east-northeast of extreme Northern Luzon on Sept. 7, 2026.
JMA via Himawari satellite

MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon will keep parts of Luzon rainy on Monday, September 7, with Zambales, Bataan, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro facing the highest risk of flash floods or landslides from moderate to heavy rain.
State weather bureau PAGASA forecasts occasional rain over the four provinces as the habagat continues to affect Luzon and the Visayas.
Metro Manila, the Ilocos Region, Abra, Benguet, Antique and the rest of Central Luzon, Calabarzon and Mimaropa may experience cloudy skies with scattered rain and thunderstorms.
Moderate to at times heavy rain in these areas may also trigger flash floods or landslides.
The rest of Luzon and the Visayas may see isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to the southwest monsoon, while localized thunderstorms may affect Mindanao.
Rivers under watch
PAGASA's 6 a.m. flood advisories identified waterways in several provinces that may still be affected by rain.
In Central Luzon, these include rivers and tributaries in Bataan and Zambales, as well as all rivers and tributaries in Bulacan.
In Calabarzon, PAGASA is monitoring river systems in Cavite, Batangas, Rizal and Laguna, including the upper Marikina and Kaliwa rivers in Rizal.
Waterways in Pangasinan and La Union also remain under watch, while river systems in Oriental Mindoro, Occidental Mindoro and Palawan may be affected by light to moderate rain or thunderstorms.
Residents near mountain slopes, waterways and low-lying areas were advised to remain alert for possible flash floods.

PAGASA, however, issued its final flood advisory for the Cordillera Administrative Region, saying waterways earlier monitored in Ifugao, Benguet and Mountain Province were no longer expected to be affected unless significant rain develops.
'Krovanh' outside PAR
A tropical storm with international name "Krovanh," formerly Pilandok, remained outside the Philippine area of responsibility as of 3 a.m.
It was located 1,155 kilometers east-northeast of extreme Northern Luzon, packing maximum sustained winds of 65 kph and gusts of up to 80 kph.
Krovanh was moving eastward at 10 kph.
Moderate to strong southwesterly to westerly winds may affect Northern Luzon, with coastal waters ranging from moderate to rough and waves reaching up to 2.8 meters.

articles.title: Several killed in Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
articles.summary: At least five people have died after a cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport. The aircraft overran a runway, struck several vehicles and caught fire.

image.caption: The Federal Aviation Administration said Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the runway while landing around 2 p.m. local timeImage: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.

The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. local time, or 18:00 GMT, after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials said at a press conference.

"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected," officials said, adding that it was too soon to determine whether those killed were on the plane or in vehicles struck by the aircraft.
According to the authorities, the crash sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit, as well as some people in cars.
Investigation launched into cause of crash
The Prime Air aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."

The flight was operated by 21 Air, a North Carolina-based cargo carrier. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to Flightradar24.
Amazon said it would cooperate with the investigation.

blocks.caption: The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami to investigate. Amazon said it would cooperate with the investigationImage: Marco Bello/REUTERS

blocks.text: “We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said in a statement. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones and all those affected by this devastating loss."
About 250 flights were delayed at the airport by late Sunday afternoon, according to FlightAware. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak several hours later, according to reports.
Eyewitness say they saw 'thick black smoke billowing into the sky'
Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, told news agencies that he went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences.
"We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it," Lee said. "I never thought it could come this close to us."

articles.title: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'
articles.summary: Peat fires in Borneo are releasing ancient stores of carbon - and sending a toxic smog across South East Asia.

blocks.text: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'
ByAhmad Dhani
Reporting fromBanjarbaru, Kalimantan
Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBC
Fahrin Ramadhianto has been fighting Borneo's wildfires for a month - and noticing the impacts on his body.

The sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur.
Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil.
It's like tear gas, says Dwi Sujatmoko.
"It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right."

The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front.

Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July.
Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes.

"Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fires have torched some 200,000 hectares across Indonesian Borneo since early July

blocks.text: Fires have torched some 200,000 hectares across Indonesian Borneo since early July
Indonesia is in the throes of a wildfire catastrophe.

Amid a so-called "Super El Niño" that has supercharged local drought conditions, thousands of active fire hotspots are spreading and multiplying across the country, fuelling a transnational haze crisis that is the region's worst in more than a decade.
But what makes Borneo's fires particularly worrying is the fact that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems.
This 4.5-million-hectare swathe of forest and swamp, under normal conditions, serves as a valuable reservoir for ancient carbon.

When these peatlands catch fire, they risk releasing millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane into the atmosphere – a "pulse" of greenhouse gas emissions that has earned them the sobriquet of "carbon bomb".

"Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).
"But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere.

"Tropical peatlands in Indonesia are among the world's most effective natural carbon stores. The deeper the peat, the greater the carbon stock – and in Kalimantan, we have found peat deposits that can exceed 20 metres in depth."

A peatland that deep has been known to harbour more than 6,000 tonnes of carbon – roughly equivalent to the annual CO₂ emissions of 4,800 cars – per hectare. And when it burns, says Dr Nisa, that fossilised carbon can be released into the atmosphere "very rapidly".

blocks.caption: Image caption, "We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty," says firefighter Dwi Sujatmoko

blocks.text: "We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty," says firefighter Dwi Sujatmoko
The toxic cloud
Thousands of people across South East Asia are now feeling the effects of those emissions in their eyes, chests and throats.

Across Indonesia as well as Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, air pollution indices have soared to "unhealthy" extremes - almost 75 times the World Health Organization's recommended level, in some cases – and hospital admissions have surged.

Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires. More than 12,000 of them were children under the age of five.

"Everybody who's living within that pollution cloud is breathing in the products of those smouldering peat fires," says Susan Page, a professor at the University of Leicester's school of geology and the environment, who's been researching peatlands in Asia for three decades.

"They're breathing in carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and they're breathing in the very finely divided particulate matter... [which] can pass through the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream and cause further problems elsewhere in the body, including issues with the heart.
"Living in this kind of pollution cloud is extremely unhealthy."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge"

blocks.text: Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge"
Nowhere are these health impacts being felt more acutely than at the coalface of the disaster: the fire front.

Here, volunteer firefighters have been risking their lives and lungs to extinguish burning peatlands which are notoriously difficult to put out. Two volunteers in Central Kalimantan have died in recent days, reportedly after their health deteriorated from putting out fires.
Cloaked in toxic haze that can burn years off a person's lifespan, volunteers have been digging ponds, canals and borewells through bone-dry peat in a desperate attempt to keep their hoses tapped.

Some have been driving pipes into the earth, making ad hoc irrigation systems to combat subterranean fires. Others have been sleeping within a stone's throw of the frontline so they can battle the blazes through the night.
"The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto, a volunteer firefighter in South Kalimantan's Banjarbaru, one of the worst-hit areas.
"The smell is like decaying wood being burned – that's the characteristic smell of peat. And that peat contains decomposed wood and organic material from many different sources."
An unnatural imbalance
Indonesia's peatland fires are not a new phenomenon.

Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.
Yet authorities have historically avoided blaming industrial actors for causing large-scale fires.

Instead, the same indigenous communities who are now engaged in firefighting operations across the island have often been accused of triggering the blazes, due to traditional farming methods that use controlled burns to clear away vegetation.

Tono, a representative of the Dayak Kanayatn people of West Kalimantan, told the BBC that Dayak communities are frequently used as scapegoats, despite carrying out land clearing with extensive planning, caution and adherence to multi-generational customs.
Tono says these communities' traditional practices, known as uma bukit or "hill farming", are rooted in the idea of maintaining balance with nature.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto

blocks.text: "The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto
But the natural balance is fast unravelling in Kalimantan, the most deforested area in Indonesia.
The region lost almost 160,000 hectares of forest area in 2025, more than one-third of the nationwide figure – much of it to make way for plantations and monocrop agriculture.
It is these same industrial-scale development projects that have been largely responsible for draining the area's peat swamps, which renders them significantly more fire-prone, Prof Page says.

"Peatlands aren't really the ideal place to set up a plantation – but of course, once the more suitable mineral soils had been exhausted it became possible, by using large machinery, to drain the peatlands and create conditions which would be dry enough," she says.
"So not only have you got the deforestation, but peatland drainage of course has also greatly increased the fire risk."
Page also points out that, whether on fire or not, a drained peatland emits carbon dioxide into the atmosphere "all of the time".

"I think that's forgotten," she says. "I think it's important to recognise that when we see the fires, they're like a dramatic example of what is actually going on the whole time in a drained peatland... The fires are just the worst expression of [that]."

Now, as these latest fires continue to spiral out of control, Sujatmoko and others face a concatenation of difficulties in the coming days, weeks and months – not least of which is a shortage of water.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Drainage and drought in Indonesia's peatlands has exacerbated their vulnerability to fire

blocks.text: Drainage and drought in Indonesia's peatlands has exacerbated their vulnerability to fire
Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge", Sujatmoko explains.
Even then there is a high chance the fire will reappear, like a smoking revenant, fed by hidden fuel buried in the invisible depths of the peat swamp.
In the face of these persistent reignitions, ongoing drought conditions and toxic smog, fatigue is another concern.
"We're definitely tired," says Sujatmoko.

"We get exhausted, we miss our families, our children, our wives. But for now, all of us are putting those things aside. We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty."
"We also hope rain comes soon," he adds. "We've spent months away from home... May all the efforts of those on the front lines be a blessing for everyone."
Additional reporting by Faisal Irfani from BBC Indonesian.

articles.title: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
articles.summary: As exam scandals persist, critics ask whether fixing the centralised testing agency is enough or if the model needs to change.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Millions of students appear for tests conducted by India's National Testing Agency every year
ByNikita Yadav
BBC News, Delhi
In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations.
Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations.

Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research.
But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own.

In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister.
In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system.
For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu.

A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented.
The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses.
Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink.

blocks.caption: Image caption, More than two million students appeared for the NEET-UG retest

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
More than two million students appeared for the NEET-UG retest

BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible.
"Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC.
"We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres."
But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says.
Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government.

"When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains.
Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed.

Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages.
Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says.
"Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The NEET-UG paper leak triggered massive protests in India

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
The NEET-UG paper leak triggered massive protests in India
Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places.
India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University.
"This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says.

For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation.
Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak.
"It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said.
The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures.
"The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again."
Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs.
The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects.
Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September.

"I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?"

blocks.caption: Image caption, Student activists and opposition parties have been demanding to scrap the NTA

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
Student activists and opposition parties have been demanding to scrap the NTA
Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether.
Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem.
The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator.

"A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency.
Rao agrees.
"It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said.
What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system.
Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself.
Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities.

The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future."
Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions.
Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system.
But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see.
"I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student.
"In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

articles.title: Assailant lunged at Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, campaign says
articles.summary:
Team says armed suspect attacked Amy Acton during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people

Amy Acton, Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, was the target of an attack…

blocks.text: Amy Acton, Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, was the target of an attack on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, campaign officials said. Several people were injured when the armed assailant lunged at Acton.
The suspect knocked volunteers to the ground before he was arrested and was “discovered to have weapons”, Mahoning county Democratic party chairperson Chris Anderson said in a statement.
Acton was not injured, but campaign officials said multiple people were hurt.

She is “grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured. This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another,” said Addie Bullock, communications director for the campaign.
A photo shared to social media by a fair attendee after the incident showed Acton checking on one of those injured in the incident.
“What happened at our tent today during today’s visit from Dr Acton is reprehensible and should be condemned by leaders on all sides of the aisle,” Anderson said.

Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton, the state’s former public health director.
Ramaswamy called the incident Sunday unacceptable.

“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement on Sunday.
Abdul El-Sayad, Michigan’s Democratic US Senate candidate, also denounced the attack.
after newsletter promotion

“There’s no place for political violence in America,” El-Sayad said in a social media post. “Our prayers go out to Dr. Acton and her team, and we hope that this moment is yet another wake up call regarding how important it is to make sure that democracy is a process by which we address our political differences peacefully.”

The fairground’s police department referred inquiries to the Mahoning county sheriff’s department, which didn’t immediately return a message seeking comment. The Ohio state highway patrol didn’t immediately respond to a request for information.
