articles.title: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran
articles.summary:
Chris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons

US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able…

blocks.text: US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”

He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.

He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.

In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.

This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.

Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.

“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.

“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.

Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.

Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.

Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

articles.title: Far-right AfD party takes big lead in regional German election
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany party has a strong lead in a regional election, but it is unclear whether it will be able to form the country's first far-right state government since the Second World…

image.caption: Election workers count ballots at a polling station in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sunday. (Liesa Johannssen/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The Alternative for Germany party has a strong lead in a regional election, but it is unclear whether it will be able to form the country's first far-right state government since the Second World War, exit polls indicated Sunday.
Results could overcome firewall of major parties refusing to work with AfD

Alternative for Germany, or AfD, went into the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern on its own. That would overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties' refusal to work with the AfD.

A first state government would be the biggest prize in the party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with an unpopular national government that has yet to persuade voters it can get the country's sluggish economy moving. It would be at least a symbolic blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.
The polls for ARD and ZDF public television put the AfD on around 44 per cent of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.

That was far ahead of Merz's Christian Democratic Union, which was seen polling 18.5 per cent and losing about half its support. The centre-left Social Democrats and Greens also were on course to remain in the state legislature, with around eight to nine per cent each.
How Germany’s AfD escaped the far-right fringe in Saxony-Anhalt
It was unclear whether the left-wing BSW party would get the five per cent of the vote needed to win seats. The exit polls put the AfD at least marginally short of an absolute majority.
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's charismatic 35-year-old candidate for state governor, told ARD that "we have written history." Voters, he said, had sent a signal that "things cannot carry on like this."

blocks.text: He said that the unpopular Merz had been "a very good campaigner for us."
Franziska Hoppermann, the national general secretary of Merz's CDU, said that it was "a very difficult result for us."
AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany's national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located.

articles.title: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks
articles.summary: The comments came a day after Washington said it had struck Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran's attacks on US warships in the region.

blocks.text: Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has denied the claim.
"The report came from Iranian state media and it's a total lie," said Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, according to the Associated Press.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued his own threats back at Iran, writing on social media on Saturday, "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."
A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, and that period of relative calm was shattered when the US resumed attacks last Sunday.

Fighting has continued throughout the week, with the US launching multiple strikes on Iranian targets and Iran retaliating against US targets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.

US President Donald Trump said this week that the renewed fighting would not last "too long", echoing comments both he and his administration have frequently made since the now six-month-long war began in February.
Months of negotiations between the US and Iran have not amounted to lasting peace, and there's little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon.
The Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to the world's oil and gas industry, has been effectively closed since the war began, and has become a major source of leverage for Iran.
Tehran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway.
But Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.

The conflict in the strait has led to an increase in gas prices globally, and ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers.
The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US hit $5.85 on Friday, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that an average of 9 million barrels of oil a day were passing through the strait, which could help ease pressure on energy prices.
Wright told CNN with oil also moving through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows".
In an interview with ABC This Week on Sunday, Wright added that gas prices should start to come down for Americans as summer demand begins to wane after Labor Day.

articles.title: Trump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loom
articles.summary:
Legal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm elections

The Trump administration renewed its appeal to the

blocks.text: The Trump administration renewed its appeal to the US supreme court on Sunday to allow restrictions on mail-in voting, after a federal judge had blocked new limits on such ballots, just ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The latest filing follows a decision by US district court judge Indira Talwani on Friday to extend a court order preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Donald Trump’s executive order.
The legal fight was continuing as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail – giving the administration little time to make major changes to the rules.

“Ballots have already begun to be mailed in North Carolina, and more states will begin the mailing process as the injunction remains in place – including Alabama on September 9 and at least five states the week of September 13,” the solicitor general, John Sauer, said in the filing to the supreme court on Sunday.

“Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them. And while the injunction allows the Postal Service and the states to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements … each day the injunction is in place risks sowing confusion and chaos because the injunction makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory,” Sauer continued in the emergency application.
It is the third time the administration has asked the highest court in the US to step into the dispute and that court has allowed the plan to move forward but has not decided whether it was legal.
The outcome of the wrangling could have significant consequences for this year’s elections, with control of Congress on the line. Nearly one-third of US voters cast their ballots by mail.

The US president signed an executive order in March that would prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots – ie only to voters on approved lists.

Democratic states and voting rights groups argue the ordered changes are unconstitutional, while state election officials who run the elections say there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives.

The Trump administration has called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” which are aimed at protecting voting security, and further called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”.

Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite having often used the method himself. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, while promoting baseless claims of fraud.

The USPS has said it stands ready to implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted.

articles.title: German far-right set for big win in eastern state - exit polls
articles.summary: Germany's AfD has hailed a "historic result" and is projected to win 44.5% of the vote, far ahead of the conservative CDU on 18.5%.

blocks.text: Germany's AfD is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, exit polls say. It is not yet clear if that would be enough to take power in the state but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.
The far-right party is projected to win 44-44.5% of the vote, far ahead of the conservative CDU on 18.5%.
The AfD has hailed the result as a "historic outcome" and the charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, has refused to rule with any other party.
No far-right party has won control of a state in Germany since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "far-right extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund.

The AfD's projected result is higher than earlier opinion polls suggested, but it will depend on which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament before the party's leaders know if they have enough seats to govern.
That may hinge on whether one of the smaller parties gets over the required threshold of 5%. If it fails, then the AfD's chances of a majority increase.

articles.title: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majority
articles.summary:
Exit poll shows Alternative für Deutschland on 44.5% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being counted

The populist far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für…

blocks.text: The populist far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, but it remains unclear as to whether it will be able to form a government and become the first far-right party to gain power at regional or parliament level since the second world war.

Initial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.5% of the vote, decisively ahead of the Christian Democrats of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world.

The CDU was trailing massively on 18.5% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.5%, with the Social Democrats on 8% and the Greens on 9%. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations.
Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.

Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority, the condition it has said is central to it taking power, as it refuses to govern with another party.

The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer, or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents. Polling booths opened at 8am local time and closed at 6pm, when exit polls were released.

Final polls before the vote had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support. The party ended up doing even better than predicted but according to initial results appears to have fallen short of the goal of its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, to gain 45% or more.
Siegmund has consistently said he would refuse to take over as state premier unless his party gained an absolute majority, saying this was the only way it could effectively enact change in Germany.
The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.

In a reflection of the significance of the vote for the entire German political landscape, the level of voter participation was considerably higher than at previous elections, hitting 54% by 2pm, compared with 27% at the same time for the equivalent vote five years ago, according to the state election commissioner.
The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.
At a final rally on Saturday, he told supporters: “No matter the outcome of tomorrow’s election, ​we have already made history.”

blocks.caption: Siegmund celebrating with the AfD’s co-leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right) after polls closed on Sunday. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is unpopular, along with his government – a coalition with the SPD – having failed in his promises so far to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to the extent that it has appeased the average voter.
A win for the AfD puts huge pressure on Merz. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has it eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.
after newsletter promotion

If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms.
He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.

Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie” or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically.

Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.

Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations planned. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.
On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”

The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.

The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.

Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

articles.title: Taguig ‘meddling’ on reclamation inspection hit
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has accused the Taguig local government of blocking the investigation by his office of alleged illegal reclamation activities in the city.

blocks.text: September 7, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has accused the Taguig local government of blocking the investigation by his office of alleged illegal reclamation activities in the city.

Speaking in his “Executive Session” program on radio dzRH on Saturday, Remulla disclosed that some personnel of the ombudsman – particularly police assigned to them – were scolded and prevented by Taguig local government personnel from taking pictures during an inspection of the reclaimed area.

“We had investigators who were being hindered in Taguig… they even identified themselves as Office of the Ombudsman personnel, to no avail,” he said. “They were supposed to fly the drone to take pictures, but they are being prevented. They are blocking cops detailed to us.”

Citing a social media post by Sen. Panfilo Lacson who divulged the alleged anomalies in reclamation projects at portions of Laguna de Bay located in the city, the Pilipino Star Ngayon reported that Special Action Force operatives arrested personnel from Taguig’s Public Order and Safety Office (POSO) for allegedly preventing ombudsman personnel from carrying out their supposed probe.

Lacson has cited eight reclamation sites along the Taguig side of the Laguna de Bay were fraudulent, four of which had fake land titles while the remaining four had no plotted lots in the digital file of the Land Registration Authority.
In a statement, the Taguig city government argued “the POSO personnel had no intention of interfering with, or preventing, the Office of the Ombudsman from carrying out its official functions.”

“Their actions were undertaken in the course of their regular public safety and enforcement duties and were prompted by the need to verify the identity and purpose of individuals who, at the time, were in civilian clothes, using an unmarked vehicle parked along a bike lane, and operating a drone in a public area,” it added.?

image.caption: Vehicles, including tourists from Alberta and Quebec, plow through an overflowing brook on Route 4 near River Bourgeois in Richmond County, N.S., Saturday. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

Even though flood waters were receding, the state of emergency declared in three counties and the Town of Port Hawkesbury remained in place Sunday, although there was some hope it could be lifted in Victoria County.
State of emergency possibly being lifted in less-impacted Victoria County
A state of emergency remained in place across much of Cape Breton on Sunday after northeastern Nova Scotia was battered by wind and a heavy rain storm.
But there was some hope that state of emergency could be lifted in the island's central and northern areas on Sunday night.
Warden Lois Landry said Richmond County on the island's southeast corner bore the brunt of the weekend storm.
"We're a community that has experienced hurricanes regularly over our history," she said Sunday afternoon.
"I think [it's] safe to say we would get at least one a year. This one seems to have hit differently.
"We saw trees down across roads on people's property. That's really Category 1 hurricane-level damage and that just wasn't in the forecast."
The storm brought strong winds and rainfall totals upwards of 200 millimetres in several communities, but it was not forecast to be nor was it declared a hurricane.
However, it wreaked havoc on roads and bridges Friday night and Saturday across the island, including the heavily populated Cape Breton Regional Municipality.
CBRM escaped the worst of the storm though, with some streets and roads closed due to rising water being reopened later in the day Saturday.
Richmond, Inverness and Victoria counties declared a state of emergency Saturday, along with the Town of Port Hawkesbury.
Trees were knocked down, there were widespread power outages and streams and ditches overflowed just about everywhere, but in some cases little damage was left behind.
Two communities in different parts of Richmond County, River Bourgeois and St. Georges Channel on West Bay Road, remained cut off by wash-outs Sunday.
Landry said that's a priority concern for emergency access, but there are also questions about the infrastructure underneath roads and bridges that got submerged and appear to be OK.
"We have had road washouts before. We have had power outages before that have not required a state of emergency," she said.
"What gave us pause and what directed our action in this instance was really not having a confident sense that the roads we were driving on, the bridges we were driving over, were safe."
Municipality 'staggered' by storm
The storm also seems to have produced one fatality, although RCMP would not confirm the cause of death.
Landry said the province and the municipality are still assessing the storm damage.
"We're staggered by the extent of the damage and the likelihood of what all that's going to cost," she said.
"All of that pales in comparison to waking up and getting confirmation of a death of a resident as a result of this weather event."

Residents are rallying around each other to help out, Landry said, including those who volunteered to stay up overnight to warn motorists about compromised roads in areas where there wasn't time or resources to put up barricades.
In Inverness County, on the west side of the island, water spilled over roads, some trees were down and there were scattered power outages, said Warden Bonny MacIsaac.
However, she said, the electricity had mostly returned by Sunday afternoon and the damage was being tallied.
"The integrity of a lot of roads [is] certainly a main concern right now," MacIsaac said.
Provincial road crews busy
In an email Sunday, Public Works spokesperson Gary Andrea said highway crews have been busy.
"At one point, we had more than 120 roads closed or damaged by flooding," he said.
"Currently, 54 roads are closed. The rest have either fully or partially reopened. Eight bridges were also damaged and two will need to be replaced."
In Victoria County, which runs from the middle of Cape Breton to its northern tip, Warden Jackie Organ said residents were very lucky.
She said damage was minimal and the state of emergency might end Sunday.
"I am waiting to hear back from public works and our [emergency management] office and ... it will be probably lifted sometime this evening," Organ said.
Port Hawkesbury expects significant bill
Roads throughout much of the three rural counties are provincially owned, but most of Port Hawkesbury's streets are the town's responsibility.
Mayor Brenda Chisholm-Beaton said it will likely be days before the full impact of the storm is known in Port Hawkesbury, but the cost is likely to be significant.
A large tree fell and damaged Prince Street and the asphalt will need to be repaired near the corner of Old Sydney Road and Bernard Street.
The town is built on a hill leading down to the Strait of Canso, so low-lying areas got submerged by runoff from the rain, Chisholm-Beaton said.

articles.title: Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill several despite truce
articles.summary: Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun has appealed to the international community to "take immediate action to stop these violations" of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon.

image.caption: One of the buildings that was destroyed was a home in Arab Salim villageImage: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: At least four people were killed in Israeli strikes on Lebanon on Sunday, which comes despite a ceasefire between the two countries, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.
The Lebanese officials also said around 20 other people, including children, were wounded in the strikes.
The office of Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun called the strikes a "dangerous escalation" that targeted "purely civilian administrations and health centers."

"President Aoun held the Israeli side fully responsible for this ongoing escalation, calling on the United States and the international community to take immediate action to stop ​these violations and hold the perpetrators accountable," his aides said in a statement.
In turn, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the strikes were a response to "a blatant violation" by Hezbollah militants.

"Terrorists from the Hezbollah terrorist organization launched two drones towards IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone in southern Lebanon," the military said in a statement, adding that there were no reports of Israeli soldiers wounded.
What do we know about the strikes?
Early on Sunday morning, the Israeli military issued an online evacuation alert for Arab Salim, saying it identified a "Hezbollah facility" there.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said the Israeli military subsequently carried out a strike on the building mentioned in the original evacuation warning.
NNA also reported that "enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it." Two women were killed in the strike.

blocks.caption: Two women were reportedly killed by Israeli strikes on Arab Salim villageImage: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another two people were killed in Israeli strikes near the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which lies on the edge of Israel's "security zone" that it occupies in southern Lebanon.
Lebanon's Health Ministry said an Israeli strike "totally destroyed" a disused hospital. The Health Ministry called the incident "another grave violation of international humanitarian law."
The Israeli military said its targets included what it described as a Hezbollah command center inside a building that was previously used as a hospital, as well as a weapons depot.
"The strikes were carried out in response to Hezbollah’s attempted attack yesterday in the Ali Taher Ridge area and to remove threats posed by Hezbollah," it said.

articles.title: Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupts, cancelling flights at Jakarta airport and others
articles.summary: Anak Krakatau volcano erupted in Indonesia early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports as volcanic…

image.caption: Anak Krakatau spews volcanic smoke in Sunda Strait, Indonesia, on Saturday, in this drone photo released by the Geological Agency of Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources. (Badan Geologi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Anak Krakatau volcano erupted in Indonesia early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports as volcanic ash drifted across parts of western Indonesia.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra’s southern tip

Anak Krakatau volcano erupted in Indonesia early Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports as volcanic ash drifted across parts of western Indonesia.

The volcanic island located in Indonesia's Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m. local time Sunday and for 16 seconds about three hours later, Indonesia's Geological Agency said. Closed-circuit camera footage showed lava flares from the volcano.

No casualties were reported, and no evacuation order was issued. The nearest settlement is more than 16 kilometres away, but authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least three kilometres from the active crater.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra's southern tip, Indonesia's Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.

AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as six other airports, including Radin Inten II airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
Thousands of passengers affected
By Sunday evening local time, the closure had affected 467 flights in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport alone that affected about 150,000 passengers. The airport was ordered closed until 11:59 p.m.
"It’s of course an inconvenience," said Diego Urdiales, a Spanish tourist who was supposed to fly home to Madrid. "I was supposed to get input from the airline ... but so far no news."
"It’s a natural disaster, it’s a force majeure, so, what can we do?" said Michele Gouw, an Indonesian passenger. "We just have to accept it and wait for the airline and airport directions."

Indonesia's Directorate General of Civil Aviation said that it was closely monitoring the eruption's impact on air travel and co-ordinating with airlines, airport operators, air navigation services and the meteorology agency.

items: Volcanic eruption in Indonesia forces evacuations, cancelled flights

blocks.text: "Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision," Lukman F. Laisa, director general of civil aviation at the Ministry of Transportation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The eruption also disrupted services at Bali’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport and at Medan.
Volcano remains active

Indonesia's volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre identified two ash clouds using satellite imagery. One plume rose to 6,100 metres and drifted northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters. A second cloud reached 15,200 metres and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces, the southern Sunda Strait and sections of the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra.
Lana Saria, head of Indonesia's Geological Agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has intensified since July, with Sunday's eruption the strongest during that period.
The repeated eruptions indicate a continued supply of magma and volcanic gases beneath the volcano, she said, though officials can't predict whether a larger eruption will occur.
"We continue to evaluate the volcano's development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column," Saria said in a video briefing.
She said the main hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas and the ejection of hot rocks and other material around the crater area.
Anak Krakatau, which means "child of Krakatau," is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.

An eruption of Anak Krakatau in 2018 caused a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau's southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Scientists said that Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption.

articles.title: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
articles.summary:
Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to…

blocks.text: China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.

A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.

The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.

The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital.

The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.

The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.

“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
after newsletter promotion
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.

The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share ​placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco ​Corp and its subsidiaries.

The two lenders said the ​proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them ​sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks ​to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

articles.title: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports
articles.summary:
Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities

Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international…

blocks.text: Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano.
Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing.
Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday.

Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday.

The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, the airport operator, Angkasa Pura, announced. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday.
The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”.
“Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement.
“Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.”
Volcanic ash can damage jet engines – baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens.

blocks.caption: Passengers wait in the check-in lounge at Soekarno-Hatta international airport.  Photograph: Faisal Ramadhan/EPA

blocks.text: Ash ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000 feet) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said.
Several ​schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents ​suffered eye irritationand fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported.
The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could ​include cloud-seeding to promote rain.

“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference.
More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore.
Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said.

Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed.
Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited to go within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant.
With Agence France-Presse
