The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.
America’s next ‘forever war’?

For Trump, “mowing the grass” has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building and deploying large numbers of American ground troops.
At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called “forever wars” he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a “Sisyphean attrition strategy without end.” As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran’s capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one. /dl

articles.title: Prince Harry’s surprise UK return renews security row
articles.summary: LONDON — Prince Harry’s return to Britain has reignited debate about whether taxpayers should foot the bill to protect him and his family, with experts warning genuine threats likely…

blocks.text: LONDON — Prince Harry’s return to Britain has reignited debate about whether taxpayers should foot the bill to protect him and his family, with experts warning genuine threats likely exist.
The Duke of Sussex, who arrived in Britain last week with his wife Meghan and their two young children, had previously ruled out returning to his home country, citing security concerns.

The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a royal family feud and Harry subsequently waged a years-long, ultimately unsuccessful, legal battle to retain UK taxpayer-funded security while living in California.
Now back with their seven-year-old son, Prince Archie, and five-year-old daughter, Princess Lilibet, he has reportedly been pushing for reinstated police protection.
However, when the family landed August 26 at Birmingham Airport, they had private security in place rather than police officers, according to British media.
“It’s very surprising,” Scott Hamer, an ex-protection officer for Harry’s father King Charles III when he was Prince of Wales, told AFP.
“There’s probably people who are being protected now who are at less threat and risk than he is. So the question would be, why does he not receive that protection as well?”
‘Vulnerability’
Harry and Meghan, who are reportedly living in central England’s Cotswolds region, are said to have enrolled their children at private schools there for the coming academic year.
They are thought to have heightened concerns about security around the kids’ daily drop-off and collection, given that these follow predictable patterns.
“The vulnerability aspect needs to be assessed,” said Hamer.
“The fact that he’ll have to take his kids to school at the same time each day, and pick them up at the same time each day, now makes him quite vulnerable.”
Britain’s Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec) — an independent body overseen by the interior ministry — decides which politicians, royals and others get police protection.
Harry battled the ministry in the courts after Ravec downgraded his security following his 2020 North America move.
The prince lost his bid to reverse the decision, branding the 2025 dismissal of his appeal a “good old-fashioned Establishment stitch-up”.
With his return, Ravec’s risk management board will likely be re-evaluating the threat level he faces.
“It’s very real,” explained Hamer, noting it could range from international terrorism to extreme right-wing actors opposed to his marriage to mixed-race Meghan.
‘Threat’
The Sunday Times reported last week that Harry’s lawyers wrote to interior minister Shabana Mahmood in August requesting she intervene.
The paper said he had lost faith in Ravec’s ability to rule fairly on his security needs, citing sources close to him.
A government spokesperson said the protection system was “rigorous and proportionate” while noting its long-standing policy not to provide details of arrangements.
“Doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals security,” the spokesperson added.
Harry is thought to be pushing for police protection in part because private security in the UK cannot be armed.

“That’s what his argument is: that the threat against him is so great that it can only be dealt with [through] an official police protection team,” another former royal protection officer, Simon Morgan, told AFP. “He feels that he should get it.”
However, the British public appear to think otherwise.
Just six percent say the prince’s security should be fully taxpayer-funded while 63 percent believe the couple should pay for it, according to a poll last week for The i Paper.
“He’s paid for security in the States. I can’t see why he can’t pay for security here — it’s a lot less dangerous,” royal expert Andrew Lownie told AFP.
‘Lot of money’
Hamer said whether Harry was a working royal or not “shouldn’t be part of it,” noting ex-PMs get protected despite leaving office.
Lownie predicted Harry would succeed in getting some taxpayer-funded protection reinstated for the same reason.
But he noted the bill for such services has ballooned over the last decade, which has seen six prime ministers leave office — compared to just two in the prior 10 years.
“If we’re doing it for all these prime ministers, then I think we’re going to have to do it for Harry and his family. But that is going to cost a lot of money.”
Harry has consistently argued he and his family are at increased risk given he is the king’s son and due to his UK military service.
The prince completed two tours of Afghanistan and claimed in his explosive 2023 memoir “Spare” to have killed 25 Taliban fighters.
Choosing to make the high-profile admission prompted criticism at the time from some British veterans, who noted it could increase his personal security risk. /dl

articles.title: Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
articles.summary: In the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, children are more likely to die than adults. But it's not always due to the disease. Specific medicines for younger people are often…

image.caption: Children have been badly affected in the current Ebola epidemic, and treatment options for them remain limitedImage: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/REUTERS

blocks.text: The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died.

Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet, the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%.
But often, it's because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself.
"Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research," the aid organization wrote in early September.

At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak.

But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms.

blocks.caption: Children under the age of 5 are significantly more likely to die from Ebola fever than adultsImage: Benediction Murhabazi/AFP

blocks.text: Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won't be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children.

According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak.

For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff.
Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it
Ebola in Berlin

In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin's Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134.
"Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out," said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments.
The available data about the drug's impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father.

In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It's unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can't be mapped onto the larger population either.

But the test was valuable nonetheless. "The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build," Le said.
Why do such gaps in knowledge exist?
Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as "small adults."

Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women.

That's why dosages of medication can't simply be transferred from adults to children. It's also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example.
DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts

"All of this creates extra costs," said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority.

"It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults," said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. "That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women."
Biot said it's sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. "Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children," he argued.
A difficult balance

None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide.
This isn't an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed.

Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn't made for children. The WHO advised it be used "off label" for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they've observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

blocks.caption: When it comes to the development of medicines and vaccines, the first samples are often made for adult patientsImage: Thomas Lohnes/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: "When you're doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product," said Russell. "But when you're in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes."

Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. "They shouldn't be excluded from participation just like that," she said. "Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset."

Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress.
"No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda
articles.summary: Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has changed suppliers for its black cherry soda.

blocks.text: Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has stopped serving the iconic US-made black cherry soda that has been a fixture at the restaurant for decades.
The sandwich shop had struggled to maintain supply of the cola for the last eight years as the distributor cut back production due to the rising cost of aluminium.
But it didn't expect the cans to vanish permanently. Now it has switched to a locally-made version, which the venue's customers have largely embraced.
Video by Eloise Alanna

articles.title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that…

blocks.text: Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.

Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.

“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”

Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.
During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.

He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.
The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.

blocks.caption: Tan Dhesi asked Andy Burnham whether he backed the 2030 commitment to defence spending at Wednesday’s PMQs. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: “There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”

Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Javier Milei threatened oil sanctions against firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.  Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/Reuters

blocks.text: His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

articles.title: Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests
articles.summary:
Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession

The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the…

blocks.text: The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May.

The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed.

blocks.caption: Taraneh Rahimi, who has a love of horses. Photograph: Taraneh Rahimi

blocks.text: The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing.

blocks.caption: Romina Rahimi. Photograph: Romina

blocks.text: The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime.

“They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.”

Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’”

Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January.

At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.
Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent.

Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from footage of anti-government protests in Tehran in early January. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters

blocks.text: The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’”

Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.”

Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before.
“My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

articles.title: Nepal’s flood-displaced mothers struggle for privacy and care
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Pariyar, who likes to be identified by only her last name, is a breastfeeding mother who is three months into caring for a newborn who does not stop crying. On the morning of August…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Pariyar, who likes to be identified by only her last name, is a breastfeeding mother who is three months into caring for a newborn who does not stop crying.

On the morning of August 26, Pariyar fled her home in Trishuli when the floods came and is now staying with dozens of strangers under one roof, where men smoke cigarettes near where she nurses her baby and where sleep, food and privacy all arrive on somebody else’s schedule.

“We are all in the same place, so it is difficult,” she says. “There is cigarette smoke, the smell of alcohol, and the baby cannot sleep.” Pariyar says her breast milk supply has decreased since the floods, leading her to try formula. However, it seems to upset the baby’s stomach, causing her to cry even more after feeding.
“If there was a safe place, and the baby could get her vaccinations here, that would be better,” Pariyar says. “We are not getting food on time either. We are not getting enough to eat.”

Pariyar’s account is part of a much larger and unfinished crisis unfolding in the flood-hit districts along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor northwest of Kathmandu. With roads and bridges damaged by landslides, pregnant women and new mothers are among those struggling hardest to get what they specifically need—a female-friendly space to breastfeed, food timed to nursing schedule, and a way to reach emergency care if labour turns dangerous.

The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), estimates that around 4,430 pregnant women are living in the areas across the 15 municipalities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, the districts hardest hit by last week’s devastating floods.

The figure is a humanitarian planning estimate based on an affected population of about 310,000 people, rather than a headcount of individually identified pregnant women. Based on the estimate, around 492 births could be expected in the following month, with roughly 74 women potentially requiring emergency obstetric care.

Aid workers say the problem is not only the scale of it. It is that these women are being folded into a relief system built around a single, generic idea of what a displaced person needs which rarely is for a breastfeeding or postpartum mother, their privacy, or an infant’s need for anything softer than the staple dal bhat.

Pariyar’s experience is not unique. In another shelter along the same corridor, Sharmila Shrestha, 33, sleeps on a classroom floor with two children: her own 14-month-old daughter, carried back to her over a six-hour walk through the hills after the flood separated them for two or three days, and her sister-in-law’s 18-month-old son. Both the infants eat what the adults eat, because nobody has brought food that suits them.

“They aren’t giving any special food for babies,” Shrestha told the Post over phone. “We are forced to feed that same heavy adult food to the small child.” What would help most, Shrestha says, is simple: “If only we had a decent, proper place to stay. That would bring some peace of mind.”
The concern is not only how many women are pregnant, but whether they can access care when they need it.

At Trishuli Hospital, the district-level hospital serving the area, the maternity ward has become an improvised outpost of crisis medicine. Basanti Pancha, who runs the department, says the hospital has performed nine deliveries since the floods but was struggling to keep pace with everything else. Women have kept arriving for fever, reduced fetal movement and urinary tract infections in pregnancy.
“Because of the floods, our service delivery has become very difficult,” Pancha says.

Electricity is unreliable enough that staff run a generator for surgeries and now sterilise instruments in small batches by hand. Four maternity patients have been referred out in recent days—two by military helicopter, two by ambulance, including a woman with a severe wound infection after delivery.

“Previously, Kathmandu was just a two-hour road trip away,” Pancha says. “Now, by road, nobody knows how many hours it will take because of the landslides.” What used to be routine, she adds, has become “a lot of stress” for staff who have no advanced neonatal unit to fall back on if a case turns critical.
“Pregnancy itself brings a lot of natural anxiety, stress and doubt about what will happen,” Pancha says. “But the floods have added a layer of extra stress on these women.”

blocks.caption: Sexual violence and trafficking have become quiet, urgent risks, worsened by the number of families now scattering toward Kathmandu in search of help that never arrived locally. Post Photo

blocks.text: Rekha Shrestha, executive director of women’s rights organisation WOREC, says her team members are finding the same pattern across every holding centre they visit: women, men, children, the sick and healthy all are sharing one undivided space. The holding centre at Chandrawati Secondary School, for instance, houses more than 1,000 people, including over 500 women, among them pregnant women and new mothers.

“Everyone is in the same place,” Rekha says. Her organisation has begun setting up female friendly spaces in affected areas, where women and adolescents can talk privately and raise concerns they would not otherwise voice in a crowded hall.
Relief distribution, she says, has often assumed everyone in a shelter needs the same things.

Menstruating adolescents are not given sufficient sanitary pads. In one distribution, she says, women were handed a single pad and told it should last three or four days. Sexual violence and trafficking have become quiet, urgent risks, worsened by the number of families now scattering toward Kathmandu in search of help that never arrived locally.

“Pregnant women and postpartum mothers have special needs,” she says. “There is no private space to bathe, to dry clothes, to breastfeed. That privacy is not an extra service in a disaster response,” she adds. “It’s a necessity.”

Rekha says her organisation is pressing officials to separate vulnerable groups within shelters, disaggregate population data by gender and age, and ensure nutrition and medicine reach women who are otherwise kept into a single, undifferentiated relief effort. “It is extremely necessary to look at the diversity within the group,” she says.

UNFPA, too, describes its 4,430 figure as only an initial estimate, one it is refining with the Ministry of Health and Population and the Health Cluster. The number is modelled, not counted door to door, derived from a pre-flood population of roughly 310,000 across the affected municipalities. “We’ve used a standard demographic ratio for how many women in a given population are likely to be pregnant at any time,” says Sriram Haridass, UNFPA’s representative in Nepal. Teams are now working to identify and reach those women individually, a process he says will take weeks. For now, the priority is keeping maternity services running while the referral system is rebuilt.

“Babies do not wait for roads to reopen,” Haridass says. UNFPA is supporting mobile health teams offering antenatal and postnatal care and psychosocial support, and has dispatched 2,000 dignity kits, 800 Kishori kits and 300 shelter tarpaulins, with 32 reproductive health kits ready for deployment. But locating a woman, Haridass says, is only half the task. “She must know where to seek care and have a functioning referral pathway if she needs urgent assistance,” he says.

That gap, between being counted and being cared for, is what women like Pariyar and Sharmila Shrestha are still living inside. Neither of the nursing mothers is asking for much: a place that treats them as something other than one more body in a crowded hall. “This is very difficult for us,” Pariyar says. “We need a separate space.” /dl

articles.title: Floods revive questions over an abandoned Nepal mountain airstrip
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When devastating floods tore through the river basins lying at Rasuwa and Nuwakot last week, reaching the affected areas by air became a challenge of its own. The landscape had been…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When devastating floods tore through the river basins lying at Rasuwa and Nuwakot last week, reaching the affected areas by air became a challenge of its own.

The landscape had been altered by landslides and flooding, while there was no air traffic control tower to coordinate the dozens of military and civilian helicopters involved in the rescue effort. During the emergency, helicopters had to operate under military supervision from an open area at the Nepal Army’s training center in Trishuli.
The disruption has revived memories among veteran aviation officials and pilots of an airstrip that has been largely forgotten by a younger generation: Langtang airport.

For those who came of age after Nepal’s political transition in 1990, the airport is little more than a name in official records. But for older aviation professionals, its short, rough runway in the mountains of Rasuwa represents something that could have been valuable during the latest disaster.
The crisis has revived debate over whether an operational Langtang airport could have eased the pressure on helicopter rescue operations.

Five helicopter trips carrying people or relief supplies could potentially have been replaced by a single small aircraft flight, while an operational airport with communications and air traffic management infrastructure could also have helped organize helicopter movements more efficiently.

“If the Langtang airport had been operational, it could have provided significant support for relief and rescue operations,” said Gyanendra Bhul, an information officer for the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and an air traffic controller.

The scale of the aviation operation during the disaster illustrates the potential value of such an alternative. Military and civilian flight records show nearly 1,000 take-offs and landings in Trishuli and surrounding areas over the course of a week.

With an airstrip capable of handling small, 19-seat aircraft and equipped with communications facilities, authorities might have reduced some of their dependence on helicopters to search for hundreds of missing people, transport relief supplies and carry out charter flights.
It could also have created room for more helicopter operations by taking some of the transport burden off them.

That makes the story of Langtang more than the history of a closed airport. It raises a broader question about how governments assess infrastructure in a country repeatedly exposed to earthquakes, floods and landslides.
Lalit Bikram Shah, a former director general of the aviation department, said the value of an airport should not be judged only by the revenue it generates during normal operations.
The lives it can help save during a disaster also have to be considered, he said, even though such a value cannot be measured in cash.
Several decades ago, single-engine Pilatus Porters operated from the airstrip, carrying tourists, project supplies and charter passengers into a part of Rasuwa that had no road access.
At the time, the airport itself was major infrastructure.

Today, Langtang remains listed in the official records of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, including with an International Civil Aviation Organization airport code, merely as “airport not in operation”.
The airport sits at an elevation of 3,658 meters, or about 12,000 feet, above sea level. Its runway is 420 meters long and 30 meters wide and has an unpaved surface.
There is no fuel facility, rescue service or fire-fighting service, according to the authority’s current airport records.
On paper, the airport still exists. In an emergency, however, it cannot be used as an operational air link.
That distinction has become particularly stark after the latest floods.
Langtang’s aviation history began not with large aircraft but with the small, single-engine Pilatus Porter, a rugged aircraft capable of operating from short mountain runways.
Shah, 81, who became the first Nepali to serve as a regional director of the International Civil Aviation Organization, remembers the airport before it fell into disuse.
Regular scheduled passenger services were not necessarily its most important function. Charter flights, development projects and flights operated for various organizations were central to its role.
“Passenger charter flights were also operated,” Shah told Kantipur on Friday, recalling the period before 1990.
Foreign development projects used the airstrip to transport equipment and supplies. Essential goods, including food, could also be flown into the remote mountain region.

Shah remembers four Pilatus Porters operated by then Royal Nepal Airlines, as well as aircraft operated by the United Nations Development Program and the US government, conducting specialized operations from Langtang.
The aircraft were suited to the short runway and difficult terrain.
Former Nepal Airlines pilot Kundan Giri remembers a similarly active airstrip, with flights carrying tourists as well as local charter passengers, project supplies and relief material.
“If the airport had remained operational, this disaster would have been easier to manage,” said Giri, a senior captain. “An airport from which aircraft can operate is a lifeline.”
Giri said the runway could be approached from either direction and that there had been potential to extend it if necessary.
A larger aircraft was once considered
There had even been attempts to determine whether Langtang could accommodate a larger aircraft.
Veteran pilot Phizo Nath Nepali said studies were carried out in the late 1980s on the possibility of operating Twin Otters from Langtang and other mountain airstrips, including Syangboche.
Nepali himself landed a Pilatus at Langtang as part of efforts related to the proposal.
The transition to Twin Otter operations never materialized. After the political changes of 1990, Nepal Airlines did not have enough aircraft to start the service, Nepali said.

According to his recollection, the airport had begun operating in the 1970s, initially with foreign pilots flying the Pilatus Porter. As those pilots left Nepal, the pool of Nepali pilots willing to fly single-engine aircraft became smaller.
“The end of the Pilatus Porter in Nepal was not simply a runway issue,” Nepali said. “The generation of aircraft and pilots was also changing.”
Nepali said other pilots, including Bishal Dewan and Manoj “Juju” Shrestha, later flew Pilatus aircraft from Langtang and other short mountain airstrips.
A study around 1988 examined whether relatively modest improvements could allow Twin Otters to operate from Langtang.
According to Nepali, the conclusion was that the runway could accommodate the aircraft with some extension and improvements.
“If the runway had been extended a little, a Twin Otter could have operated there quite comfortably,” he recalled.

Local residents supported the idea, unlike in Syangboche, where some tourism operators opposed it. They feared that allowing tourists to fly directly into Syangboche would reduce the two-day trek and hurt local hotels and other businesses.
Langtang did not face the same resistance, Nepali said. /dl

articles.title: Haze emergency grips Malaysian Borneo town
articles.summary: SERIAN, Malaysia — Acrid smoke hung heavily over the Malaysian town of Serian, seeping into homes and cloaking roadside stalls, as residents navigated an air‑quality emergency fueled by…

blocks.text: SERIAN, Malaysia — Acrid smoke hung heavily over the Malaysian town of Serian, seeping into homes and cloaking roadside stalls, as residents navigated an air‑quality emergency fueled by transboundary haze from Indonesia’s raging fires.
Malaysia declared a state of emergency in Sarawak state’s Serian district on Borneo island on Friday, after air pollution readings reached critical levels.

Toxic haze has shrouded parts of Indonesia and Malaysia for weeks as Jakarta struggles to contain fires that have scorched large tracts of Borneo and Sumatra, with the plumes drifting into neighboring Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei.

In Serian, about 65 kilometers (40 miles) southeast of Sarawak’s capital Kuching, residents tried to carry on with weekend routines but said the thick haze forced them to plan shorter trips to avoid the worst of the smoke.
“I rarely leave the house when it’s like this (the haze). I only come out to buy food and groceries, then I’ll immediately head home,” said Ajen Anak Kunok, 64, a local retired technician.
Ajen told AFP he had spent the past week battling shortness of breath and a sore throat due to the ongoing haze, before going to the hospital Saturday for treatment.
But the smoke was difficult to escape even at home, a mere 10 kilometers (six miles) from Indonesia’s Kalimantan province where the fires were raging.
“Even when I turn on the air conditioner, I can still smell the smoke in my house,” Ajen said.
Hazardous levels
Sarawak, which shares a border with Kalimantan, has borne the brunt of pollution in Malaysia.
On Friday, Serian became the first district in the country this year to declare an emergency over the worsening air quality when API levels passed 500 and peaked at 512.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API levels above 300 are classified as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 usually trigger consideration of a local emergency.
At the town’s markets, the usual bustling throng dwindled, while roadside sellers of Serian’s famous durians waited in vain beside their piles of fruit for customers that came in diminished numbers.
The district’s scenic Ranchan Waterfall — usually popular with locals and tourists alike — was unusually quiet, with just a few visitors dotted around.
Roadside durian seller Siaw Thien Ha, 53, said the emergency has already hit his livelihood hard.
He struggled to earn even half of his usual income of 400 ringgit ($98) for the weekend.
“I’m worried that my income will be affected… But during the durian season, there is money to be made,” he told AFP.
“So I don’t have a choice but to bring the durians here to sell to support my family,” he said.
Friday’s emergency declaration will also keep some 647 schools closed until at least the end of the week in Serian district, which has a population of around 154,000 people.
Sister Irmina Peter, 64, who teaches at the St Joseph’s Private Primary School in Kuching, told AFP she was worried that the emergency could drag on and spill over to other districts in Sarawak.
Rain in Serian on Friday night and Saturday morning, believed to have been the result of ongoing cloud seeding operations, brought some respite, with API levels dropping to 219.
Serian’s state of emergency however remained in place.
Sister Peter said “we don’t want the schools to be like during Covid-19 lockdown, where we couldn’t do much.”
“We can’t go on with our normal routine… we have to go to work, children have to go to school. It affects us very much.” /dl

articles.title: Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
articles.summary: Hungary's new prime minister promised he would recover billions stolen or diverted by the previous administration. A new "super authority" is about to begin that work. Its success or failure will…

image.caption: In his election campaign, Peter Magyar promised to recover government funds that were stolen or diverted by the Orban administrationImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.

Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.

Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.
Orban, allies lived lives of luxury
Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.

The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.

Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.

blocks.caption: Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban has alleged that his successor has 'dismantled the rule of law' since coming to powerImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.
It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.
At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.

Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.
Hungary new PM lifts lid on Orban-era government luxury
This time, things are meant to be different.

The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.
The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.
Controversy around new anti-corruption body
But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.

Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.

Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.

blocks.caption: Anna Unger was named head of the new accountability organization in late AugustImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.

Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.
No justice in next 6 years?
Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.

Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.
The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.

"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.

In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.

Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.
This article was originally written in German.
New Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar takes on Orban's legacy

articles.title: Nigeria: Suspected oil thieves killed after inhaling fumes
articles.summary: PORT HARCOURT, Nigeria — At least 37 people died early Thursday in Nigeria’s oil-rich southern Niger Delta after inhaling fumes during the theft of fuel from a pipeline, a local NGO said.…

blocks.text: PORT HARCOURT, Nigeria — At least 37 people died early Thursday in Nigeria’s oil-rich southern Niger Delta after inhaling fumes during the theft of fuel from a pipeline, a local NGO said.
Illegal oil-siphoning is a major problem in Nigeria — an OPEC member and one of Africa’s largest petroleum producers — causing serious pollution.
Accidents are common in swamps in the Niger Delta, where smugglers tap into pipelines to steal crude and refine it into fuel for sale.

The Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre (YEAC-Nigeria) said it had “received and confirmed a report from its network of youth volunteers and human rights defenders in the Niger Delta in the Okrika Local Government Area of Rivers State that some persons, not fewer than 37 have been confirmed dead after inhaling ‘Indorama fuel’.”
It said in a statement that those killed are “suspected to be oil thieves”, adding: “Many others are still missing.”

It said “youths had connected a pipe to a tapping point on a pipeline that normally transports” crude from producer Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery to vessels loading for export.
The men tapped into the pipeline and were loading oil into their own boats, it said.
“Many are still missing, and some corpses have been seen floating on the river but have not yet been recovered,” the organisation said.
Oil pollution
Rivers State police confirmed the incident in a statement saying the victims were allegedly attempting to steal oil, but it did not give a toll.
The Niger Delta is home to Nigeria’s multi-billion-dollar oil and gas resources, but residents of the region live in poverty due to decades of oil exploration, neglect and pollution.
The opposition party African Democratic Congress blamed the accident on the “economic situation in the country” which it said forces people to take desperate action.
The party’s candidate Atiku Abubakar will challenge President Bola Tinubu in elections in January.
When he came into office in 2023, Tinubu introduced tough economic reforms that triggered high inflation, soaring fuel prices and rising poverty.
YEAC-Nigeria called “on the government to provide alternative livelihood opportunities”, including “the legalization of artisanal refining”. /dl

articles.title: Egypt sentences TV presenter, 11 others to death in drugs case
articles.summary: CAIRO — An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drugs case, official media reported on…

blocks.text: CAIRO — An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drugs case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her program “Mission Impossible”, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organized criminal gang specializing in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a plastic surgery clinic and a production company that specializes in organizing parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar Al-Youm newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.
Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750 kilograms of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025. /dl

articles.title: Israel army says striking southern Lebanon, urges evacuation
articles.summary: JERUSALEM — The Israeli military said on Sunday it was carrying out strikes in southern Lebanon after Hezbollah launched drones at its soldiers, and urged residents of the town of Arab Salim to…

blocks.text: JERUSALEM — The Israeli military said on Sunday it was carrying out strikes in southern Lebanon after Hezbollah launched drones at its soldiers, and urged residents of the town of Arab Salim to evacuate.

“Terrorists from the Hezbollah terrorist organization launched two drones towards IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone in southern Lebanon,” the military said in a statement, adding that there were no reports of Israeli soldiers wounded.
“This constitutes a blatant violation by the Hezbollah terrorist organization. In response, the IDF is now striking in southern Lebanon.”
In another message, the Israeli military warned residents of Arab Salim to leave ahead of imminent attacks.
“You are situated near a facility belonging to the terrorist organisation Hezbollah, against which the IDF will be operating,” it wrote in Arabic on Telegram.

Lebanon was drawn into the Middle East war in March after Iran-backed Hezbollah attacked Israel, which responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
Violence has lessened since a US-Iran memorandum of understanding on the broader conflict in June and a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon later that month.
Israeli forces are operating inside a self-declared “security zone” around 10 kilometers (six miles) deep inside Lebanon along the border.
Authorities in Lebanon said on Saturday that Israeli strikes killed four people in the country’s south and east. /dl

articles.title: Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
articles.summary: The spread of ash after the volcanic eruption of Anak Krakatau has impacted thousands of passengers, as flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport.

image.caption: The eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau saw lava sprouting and spewing of ash that was detected even 150 kilometers awayImage: PVMBG/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hundreds of flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday morning, more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) away.
The volcano produced a fountain of lava and loud sounds heard up to 700 kilometres (435 miles) away, Indonesia's geological agency said in a statement.

The cloud of ash was detected up to a height of 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano and a plume of up to 15,000 meters (50,000 feet) on the ‌Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the ‌meteorological ​agency BMKG posted on its website.
No incidents of casualties were reported, and no evacuation orders were issued.
Danger remains in Indonesia in the wake of volcano eruptions
The closest township is more than 16 kilometers (10 miles) away, but the authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) from the volcano's active crater.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.
Indonesia cancels flights
The ash spread across parts of the capital Jakarta and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.
The spread of ash after the volcanic eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau disrupted operations at Jakarta's international airport.
Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on ‌Instagram that it had ⁠suspended ⁠flight operations until 9:30 a.m. (0230 GMT) due to volcanic ash.
New volcano eruptions hit Indonesia
"Due to increased activity from the Mount Anak Krakatau eruption, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has temporarily suspended flight operations from 5:30 a.m. to 9.30 a.m.," the airport said.
The disruption of flight operations has impacted more than 22,000 passengers, the transport ministry said in a statement, adding that 209 flights were affected, particularly to and from Singapore.
Anak Krakatau lies in the middle between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia's vast island chain, which sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent.
Anak Krakatau means "Child of Krakatau." The volcano is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental eruption in 1883 triggered a period of global cooling.

articles.title: Indonesia’s main airport suspends operations after volcanic eruption
articles.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday due to ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano, more than 150 kilometers away. Mount Anak…

blocks.text: JAKARTA — Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday due to ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano, more than 150 kilometers away.
Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to 700 kilometres (435 miles) away, the geology agency said in a statement.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.
Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to suspend operations from 01:30 am Sunday (Saturday 1830 GMT).

“The latest paper test…showed positive results indicating the spread of volcanic ash in the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport area, consequently the airport closure was extended until Sunday at 09:30 am (0230 GMT),” the transport ministry said in a statement Sunday.
More than 22,000 passengers have been impacted by the suspension, the ministry said, adding that 209 flights were affected, in particular to and from Singapore.
Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney, and Kuala Lumpur.
Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.
It has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history with an estimated 35,000 people killed.
Indonesia, a Southeast Asian archipelago nation, sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity. /dl

articles.title: Barely saved, he cuts mourning short to help flood survivors
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Two seconds is time enough to blink. For 31-year-old Sudip Kumar Neupane, this window meant the difference between life and death. Sudip was racing back on a motorcycle after…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Two seconds is time enough to blink. For 31-year-old Sudip Kumar Neupane, this window meant the difference between life and death.
Sudip was racing back on a motorcycle after warning villagers of an approaching flood when buffaloes slowed him down by an estimated two seconds.
Then a torrent of flood and debris came.

As mud and rock and water barrelled down, carrying away his 27-year-old younger brother, Pradip, and Janak, an information technology officer in Uttargaya Rural Municipality in Rasuwa whom Neupane regarded as a cousin.
Sudip survived, only to be haunted by the question of why he lived when the two men beside him did not.

His survival by a whisker means a life tormented by the disaster. Much like hundreds of others who lost their loved ones when a glacial collapse in the Langtang region on August 26 unleashed a devastating flood on the Bhotekoshi river.

After spending two days grieving, Sudip returned to the front line of the relief effort. Displaced people needed food and shelter, and the local unit was short of staff. Some people objected to his presence in relief distribution.

Sudip kept his cool. “We are educated and responsible people. In a disaster, we need to remain calm,” he said. “I survived by luck. For as long as I live, I will continue serving society and the people.”
The morning the flood came
Sudip works as a fourth-level officer in the enterprise development section of Uttargaya Rural Municipality. On August 26, he felt an air of unease.
He did not want to go out that morning. His uncle, who worked at the District Administration Office, warned him before he left. “Son, be careful. There is a flood coming.”
But Sudip felt he had a responsibility to the people around him. As a resident and municipal employee, he believed he needed to help warn villagers of the danger.
Pradip, his younger brother who was a seventh-level public health officer in the rural municipality, joined him. The brothers set out on motorcycles to warn people.
Sudip gave his motorcycle to Pradip, who handed it to health worker Maniram and sat behind him. Sudip travelled on another motorcycle with Janak, locally known as “Janak dai”.
From behind, his younger brother Pradip called out, “Brother, we need to make an announcement!”
Hearing him, Sudip took the microphone and began warning people about the approaching flood as they moved on.

blocks.caption: Relief distribution process underway at Nilakantha Higher Secondary School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5 on Thursday.

blocks.text: At Khalte, Sudip warned Pradip not to get any farther. Pradip stopped there while Sudip and Janak continued towards Nayapul.
There they encountered Balaram Neupane, chief of the local health service, rushing back for safety.
“Friends, we won’t survive! We’ll die! Turn back, turn back!” he shouted out.
They turned around and accelerated back towards Khalte. Then came the delay that Sudip believes saved his life.
Buffaloes belonging to displaced members of the Tamang community, who were staying at a temporary camp, were blocking the road.
For roughly two seconds, according to Sudip, they could not move. When the animals cleared out, they continued towards Khalte. The flood struck from behind.
‘It came like a missile’
Sudip says what came down the valley did not feel like an ordinary flood.
“I don’t see it simply as a flood, and it wasn’t an ordinary wave,” he said. “It came like a missile, like artillery. It swept everything away. Nobody even had enough time to make a sound.”
Janak lost control of his motorcycle. He abandoned it and ran towards a field. Neupane ran uphill. The first wave was already behind them.
“Within five minutes of the flood arriving, our office was destroyed,” he said. “In those moments, chances hovered between death and survival. There was no time to pause even for breath.”

Sudip had managed to run for only four or five seconds uphill when the first wave hit. He thought his brother had escaped. Pradip was tall and long-legged. Sudip’s assumption that he could have outrun the water was wrong. He did not survive.
A brother with big dreams
Pradip was 27, had recently built a house and had many plans for the future.
“We came from a poor family. We grew up wearing worn-out clothes and eating whatever food we could afford. We worked hard to build better lives for ourselves,” Sudip recalled.
Their uncle and aunt struggled to support his education, sometimes going without meals to pay for his studies. Pradip eventually earned a master’s in public health.
‘Perhaps I survived for a reason’
Sudip earns about Rs32,000 a month as a municipal employee. The experience has changed his perception of life.
“If we both brothers had died, our family would have been shattered,” he said. “Perhaps that terrifying wave threw me out saying, ‘Now you have to take responsibility for the family.’”
That sense of responsibility helped him overcome grief while people around him were hungry, displaced and needy. “I will help them as much as I can.” /dl

articles.title: Two people rescued alive on 11th day after deadly Nepal floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Two people were rescued alive on Saturday, 11 days after devastating floods in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River left them missing. A Chinese national was rescued from Audit-4 of the Upper…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Two people were rescued alive on Saturday, 11 days after devastating floods in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River left them missing.
A Chinese national was rescued from Audit-4 of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project in Rasuwa district, the Nepali Army said.

The man had been trapped inside the tunnel since the flooding hit the area. Army spokesman Rajaram Basnet said a team from the Nepali Army, assisted by disaster experts from South Korea, carried out the rescue operation.
He was being taken to an army barracks in Trishuli, Nuwakot, for further care.

blocks.caption: Chandika Shrestha, 64, a resident of Betrawati in Bidur Municipality-10, had gone missing alongside four members of her family on August 26, when the flash floods tore through the Bhotekoshi river basin, decimating entire settlements.  Photo: Courtesy of Nepal Police

blocks.text: Separately, a 64-year-old woman was rescued alive from the upper floor of a four-storey house in Betravati, Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot.

The woman, identified as Chandika Shrestha, had been trapped after the house was buried in the floods. A nine-member rescue team from the army’s No. 19 Battalion, led by Assistant Superintendent of Police Suman Kumar BK, rescued her from the upper floor.
The two rescues came on the 11th day of search and rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi floods, which caused widespread destruction in Rasuwa and surrounding areas. /dl

articles.title: US envoys set for Ukraine talks after meeting Putin in Moscow
articles.summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner leave Moscow talks with hopes for "equally productive meetings" in Ukraine.

blocks.text: As Witkoff and Kushner were negotiating at the Kremlin, Zelensky said he was ready for "a substantive conversation".
Saturday's talks in Moscow lasted three hours and were held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital, according to Russian state media.
Details are still emerging, but both sides have given broadly positive remarks without going into specifics.
Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank".

"The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict".

Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022.

Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but given Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it is not clear how they will be travelling to Kyiv from Moscow.
The talks come after Russia and Ukraine have intensified aerial attacks in recent months.

Ukraine says it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets, notably oil installations.

articles.title: Japan Prince Hisahito, 2nd in line to throne, turns 20
articles.summary: Prince Hisahito, the nephew of Emperor Naruhito and second in line to the Chrysanthemum Throne, turned 20 on Sunday, a year after a series of traditional ceremonies commemorated his coming of age. As…

blocks.text: Prince Hisahito, the nephew of Emperor Naruhito and second in line to the Chrysanthemum Throne, turned 20 on Sunday, a year after a series of traditional ceremonies commemorated his coming of age.

As an adult member of the imperial family, the prince has taken part in royal events and performed official duties, often alongside his parents, Crown Prince Fumihito and Crown Princess Kiko, and his elder sister Princess Kako, while prioritizing his studies at the University of Tsukuba, northeast of Tokyo.
The prince feels grateful for the various support he has received from people, according to the Imperial Household Agency.

In April, he began his second year at university. He takes English classes to read biology papers and has also enrolled in specialized courses for lectures and laboratory work in the field of biology.
The prince participated in fieldwork in the summer and is active in club activities with friends.

He has a place to live in Tsukuba, Ibaraki Prefecture that is close to his university. When he returns to Akasaka Estate in Tokyo, where his family resides, he cultivates vegetables and rice and continues to observe the habitats of creatures such as dragonflies.

After completing the coming-of-age rites in September last year, the prince renewed his commitment to fulfilling his responsibilities as an adult member of the imperial family, according to the agency.

He attended imperial ceremonies such as the New Year’s Greeting and the New Year’s Poetry Reading for the first time and debuted at a state banquet hosted by Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako in May to welcome Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his wife Louise Araneta-Marcos.
At the dinner, the prince exchanged words in English with the Philippine guest seated next to him, the agency said.
Over the past year, he has visited six prefectures, including Mie and Kyoto, for trips related to the coming-of-age ritual and other purposes.
During a solo visit to Hiroshima Prefecture in August, he laid flowers at the Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims, commemorating the victims of the U.S. atomic bombing in 1945.
Visiting an exhibition about an elementary school where many children lost their lives, the prince was once again struck by the tragedy of the atomic bombing, according to the agency.
He also attended a boy scout camp gathering in Jinsekikogen in Hiroshima Prefecture and delivered a speech for the first time at an official ceremony.
In November last year, his entire family attended the opening ceremony of the Tokyo Deaflympics, an international sporting event for the deaf and hard of hearing.

He visited Izu Oshima Island in the Pacific with Crown Princess Kiko to watch a competitive event and said he was delighted to be able to interact with the athletes using the sign language he had learned, the agency said.
A close aide said the prince “carries out each event with care and converses wholeheartedly with the people he meets.”
After turning 18 in September 2024, the prince became the imperial family’s first male member to reach adulthood since his father, Crown Prince Fumihito, in November 1985.
But the official coming-of-age ceremonies were postponed by a year to avoid disrupting his university entrance exam preparations. /dl

articles.title: Watch: Moment 64-year-old Nepali woman is found alive in mud-buried home
articles.summary: Chandika Shrestha was airlifted to hospital after spending more than 10 days in her partially buried house.

blocks.text: More than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud tore through a Himalayan valley in Nepal, rescuers continue to find survivors.

Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old woman, was discovered alive on the fourth floor of her partially buried house in the Nuwakot district by Nepal's Armed Police Force on 5 September, according to Reuters.
She was airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment, Reuters reported.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact
articles.summary: The parliamentary election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government, further raising dissatisfaction with Chancellor Friedrich…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (center) made few campaign appearances in Saxony-Anhalt to support CDU Premier Sven Schulze (right)Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Only 1.6 million eligible voters are called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

Nonetheless, the vote has become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

This is because the in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party leads the polls in Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of the centrist parties governing at the federal level, the CDU and SPD. Even an absolute majority for the right-wing populists cannot be ruled out. If that came to pass, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.
A threat to Chancellor Friedrich Merz?
Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

An absolute majority for the AfD could, however, plunge the governing coalition in Berlin into crisis, Koschmieder said. It would also intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party. His Union of the CDU and CSU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.
Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.
Saxony-Anhalt election: Can the CDU stop the AfD?

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

But many other conservative politicians fear the opposite: that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.
Merz: Government stability not at risk

In other words: It is mainly for the chancellor's party that the election result in Saxony-Anhalt could become a crucial test. Merz has already identified this issue, and has made recent calls for calm.
"Outsiders are trying to drive a wedge into the Union. The result of a state parliament election does not endanger the stability of the federal government," he told the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung.
Amid far right's rise, is Germany at a breaking point?

The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.
But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.
AfD state government feared to be a security risk

Political scientist Koschmieder also thinks many CDU politicians at the state level will continue their criticism of the pension reform plans, but he added: "I do not think they will completely fail, but there will be amendments in some places."

Pressure from his own party, problems with upcoming reforms — all of this could be in store for the chancellor.
